title: Part 2, Chapter 15
paragraphs: In which it is told and made known who the Knight of the Mirrors and his squire were

Don Quixote rode away thoroughly pleased with himself, elated and swollen with pride at having triumphed over so valiant a knight as he imagined him of the Mirrors to be — a knight from whose pledged word he expected to learn whether his lady’s enchantment still held, since the defeated man was obliged, on pain of forfeiting his knighthood, to come back and report what had passed between himself and her. But Don Quixote had one thing in mind and he of the Mirrors quite another, for at that moment the latter could think of nothing except finding some village where he might apply plasters to himself, as has already been mentioned. The history then goes on to relate that when the bachelor Samson Carrasco urged Don Quixote to take up again the knight-errantry he had set aside, he did so because he had first met in private council with the curate and the barber to discuss what means might persuade Don Quixote to stay quietly and peacefully at home, untroubled by his ill-fated adventures. At that meeting it was resolved by the unanimous vote of everyone present, and on Carrasco’s particular recommendation, that Don Quixote should be allowed to set out, since holding him back seemed impossible, and that Samson should ride out to meet him as a knight-errant and fight him — finding a pretext would present no difficulty — and defeat him, this being regarded as an easy thing to accomplish; and it would be agreed and stipulated beforehand that the loser must place himself at the winner’s mercy. Then, once Don Quixote was beaten, the bachelor knight would order him to go back to his village and his house and not leave it for two years, or until he received further instructions from him — all of which, it was plain, Don Quixote would obey without hesitation rather than break or disregard the laws of chivalry; and during this period of confinement he might perhaps forget his delusions, or some effective cure for his madness might be discovered. Carrasco took on the task, and Tom Cecial, a crony and neighbor of Sancho Panza’s, a cheerful, scatterbrained fellow, volunteered to serve as his squire. Carrasco armed himself in the manner already described, and Tom Cecial, so that his old crony would not recognize him when they met, fitted over his own natural nose the false carnival one that has been mentioned; and so they followed the same road Don Quixote was traveling, very nearly catching up with him in time to witness the adventure of the cart of Death, and at last came upon the pair in the grove, where everything the attentive reader has just been reading took place. And had it not been for Don Quixote’s extraordinary delusions, and his conviction that the bachelor was not the bachelor, señor bachelor would have been disqualified forever from ever taking his licentiate’s degree — all because he found no nests where he expected to find birds.

Tom Cecial, seeing how badly things had gone and what a miserable end their expedition had come to, said to the bachelor, “Well, Señor Samson Carrasco, we got exactly what we deserved. It’s easy enough to dream up a venture and set it in motion, but coming out of it in one piece is often another matter entirely. Don Quixote is the madman and we are the sane ones — yet he rides off laughing, safe and sound, while you sit here bruised and sorry. So tell me now: who is the greater madman, the one who can’t help it, or the one who chooses it of his own free will?”

To which Samson answered, “The difference between the two kinds of madmen is this: the one who is mad whether he likes it or not will stay mad forever, while the one who is mad by his own choice can stop being mad whenever he pleases.”
“In that case,” said Tom Cecial, “I was a madman by my own choice when I volunteered to be your squire, and by my own choice I’ll stop being one and head home.”

“That’s your business,” Samson replied, “but to imagine I’m going home before I’ve given Don Quixote a sound beating is ridiculous. And it isn’t any hope of restoring his sanity that will drive me to hunt him down now — it’s the desire for revenge; for the throbbing pain in my ribs won’t allow me any more charitable thoughts than that.”

Conversing in this way, the two pressed on until they came to a town where, by good fortune, they found a bone-setter, under whose care the unlucky Samson was patched up. Tom Cecial left him there and went home, while Samson stayed behind brooding on his revenge; and the history will come back to him in due course, so as not to miss the chance of making merry with Don Quixote in the meantime.

title: Part 2, Chapter 16
paragraphs: About what happened to Don Quixote when he met a discreet gentleman of La Mancha

Don Quixote rode on in the high spirits, satisfaction, and self-congratulation already described, picturing himself the most valorous knight-errant in the world thanks to his recent victory. From now on he counted every adventure that could befall him as already accomplished and brought to a happy end. He made light of enchantments and enchanters; he stopped dwelling on the countless beatings he'd taken in the course of his career, the volley of stones that had knocked out half his teeth, the ingratitude of the galley slaves, or the audacity of the Yanguesans and the shower of stakes that had rained down on him. In short, he told himself that if he could only find some way, means, or method to disenchant his lady Dulcinea, he wouldn't envy the highest fortune any of the most fortunate knights-errant of old had ever reached or could reach.
He was riding along entirely absorbed in these fancies when Sancho said, "Isn't it strange, señor, that I still see in front of my eyes that monstrous huge nose of my pal Tom Cecial?"
"And do you actually believe, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that the Knight of the Mirrors was the bachelor Carrasco, and his squire your pal Tom Cecial?"

"I don't know what to say about that," Sancho replied; "all I know is that the things he told me about my own house, wife, and children, nobody but him could have known. And the face, once the nose was off, was the very face of Tom Cecial as I've seen it many a time in our town, next door to my own house — and the voice sounded exactly the same."

"Let's reason this out, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Tell me — by what train of thought can it be supposed that the bachelor Samson Carrasco would come dressed as a knight-errant, in offensive and defensive arms, to fight me? Have I ever, by any chance, been his enemy? Have I ever given him any reason to hold a grudge? Am I his rival, or does he practise arms, that he should envy the fame I've won in them?"

"Well, but what are we to make of it, señor," Sancho returned, "if that knight — whoever he was — looked so much like the bachelor Carrasco, and his squire so much like my pal Tom Cecial? And if that's enchantment, as your worship says, was there no other pair in the world for them to take the likeness of?"

"It is all," said Don Quixote, "a scheme and plot of the malicious magicians who persecute me. Foreseeing that I'd win the fight, they arranged for the defeated knight to wear the face of my friend the bachelor, so the friendship I bear him would step in to blunt the edge of my sword and the strength of my arm, and cool the just anger of my heart — so the man who'd come to take my life by fraud might save his own. And to prove it, Sancho, you know already, from experience that can't lie or deceive, how easy it is for enchanters to change one face into another, turning fair into foul and foul into fair. Less than two days ago you saw with your own eyes the beauty and elegance of the peerless Dulcinea in all her natural harmony and perfection, while I saw her in the repulsive, mean shape of a coarse country wench, with cataracts in her eyes and a foul stink in her mouth. And if the perverse enchanter dared work so wicked a transformation, no wonder he managed the same with Samson Carrasco and your pal, to snatch the glory of victory out of my hands. But for all that I take comfort, because in whatever shape he wore, I beat my enemy."

"God knows the truth of it," said Sancho; and knowing as he did that Dulcinea's transformation had been his own trick, his master's explanations didn't satisfy him. But he didn't dare reply, in case he let something slip that would expose his deception.

While they were having this conversation, a man overtook them, riding the same road behind them on a very handsome flea-bitten mare. He was dressed in a gaban of fine green cloth with tawny velvet facings and a montera of the same velvet. The mare's trappings were in the field and jineta style, mulberry and green. He carried a Moorish cutlass hanging from a broad green-and-gold baldric; his buskins matched the baldric; his spurs were not gilt but lacquered green, polished so brightly that, against the rest of his outfit, they looked better than if they had been pure gold.

When the traveller caught up with them he greeted them politely and was about to spur his mare past them, but Don Quixote called out, "Sir, if your worship happens to be heading our way and isn't in a hurry, it would be a pleasure to me if we travelled together."
"Honestly," the man on the mare replied, "I wouldn't pass you so quickly, except I'm afraid your horse might get skittish in the company of my mare."

"You can safely hold in your mare, señor," Sancho put in, "because our horse is the most virtuous, well-behaved horse in the world. He never misbehaves on such occasions, and the one time he did, my master and I paid for it sevenfold. Honestly, your worship can pull up if you like, because even if she were served to him between two plates, the horse wouldn't crave her."

The traveller drew rein, amazed at Don Quixote's getup and features. He rode without his helmet, which Sancho was carrying like a saddlebag in front of Dapple's pack-saddle. And if the man in green looked closely at Don Quixote, Don Quixote looked even more closely at the man in green, who struck him as a man of intelligence. He looked about fifty, with only a few grey hairs, an aquiline face, an expression somewhere between grave and cheerful, and a dress and accoutrements that marked him as well-off. What the man in green made of Don Quixote of La Mancha was that he'd never seen anyone of that sort and shape before. He marvelled at the length of his hair, his great height, the gauntness and yellow tinge of his face, his armour, his bearing, his gravity — a figure that hadn't been seen in those parts for many a long day.

Don Quixote could see perfectly well the attention with which the traveller was studying him, and read the curiosity in his astonishment. Always courteous and eager to please, he anticipated the other man's questions by saying, "The figure I present is so strange and so out of the ordinary that I shouldn't be surprised if it fills you with wonder. But you'll stop wondering when I tell you, as I do now, that I am one of those knights who, as people say, go out seeking adventures. I have left my home, mortgaged my estate, given up my comforts, and put myself in Fortune's arms to take me wherever she pleases. My desire was to revive knight-errantry, now dead, and for some time past — stumbling here, falling there, sometimes coming down headlong, sometimes picking myself up again — I have carried out a great part of my design, helping widows, protecting maidens, aiding wives, orphans, and minors, the proper and natural duty of knights-errant. And so, on account of my many valiant and Christian deeds, I've already been judged worthy to find my way in print to almost every nation on earth. Thirty thousand copies of my history have been printed, and it's on track to be printed thirty thousand thousand more times if heaven doesn't put a stop to it. To sum it all up in a single word, I can tell you that I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, otherwise known as 'The Knight of the Rueful Countenance.' Self-praise is degrading, I know, but sometimes I have to sound my own — that is, when there's no one at hand to do it for me. So, kind sir, neither this horse, nor this lance, nor this shield, nor this squire, nor all these arms together, nor the yellowness of my face, nor my gaunt leanness, need astonish you any longer, now that you know who I am and what profession I follow."

With these words Don Quixote fell silent, and from the time it took the man in green to reply, he seemed at a loss for what to say. After a long pause, however, he said, "You were right when you saw curiosity in my amazement, sir knight, but you haven't managed to remove the astonishment I feel at seeing you. You say, señor, that knowing who you are should remove it, but it hasn't done so; on the contrary, now that I know, I am left more amazed than before. What — is it possible there are knight-errants in the world in these days, and histories of real chivalry being printed? I can't take it in that there's anyone on earth nowadays who aids widows, protects maidens, defends wives, or rescues orphans; nor would I believe it if I hadn't seen it in your worship with my own eyes. Blessed be heaven! By means of this history of your noble and genuine chivalrous deeds, which you say has been printed, the countless tales of fictitious knight-errants that fill the world — to the damage of morals and the discredit of true history — will be driven into oblivion."
"There's plenty to be said on that point," said Don Quixote, "as to whether the histories of the knight-errants are fiction or not."
"Why, is there anyone who doubts those histories are false?" said the man in green.

"I doubt it," said Don Quixote, "but never mind that for now. If our journey lasts long enough, I trust in God I'll show your worship that you're wrong to go along with the crowd that takes it for certain they're not true."

This last remark of Don Quixote's left the traveller suspecting that he was some kind of madman, and waiting for him to confirm it with something further. But before they could turn to a new subject, Don Quixote asked him to say who he was, since he himself had given an account of his station and life. To this the man in the green gaban replied, "Sir Knight of the Rueful Countenance, I am a gentleman by birth, born in the village where, God willing, we'll dine today. I am more than reasonably well-off, and my name is Don Diego de Miranda. I spend my life with my wife, children, and friends. My pastimes are hunting and fishing, but I keep neither hawks nor greyhounds — just a tame partridge and one or two bold ferrets. I have six dozen or so books, some in our mother tongue, some in Latin, some history, some devotional. Books of chivalry have not yet crossed my threshold; I lean more toward the secular than the devotional, so long as they're books of honest entertainment that charm by their style and attract by the invention they show — though of those there are very few in Spain. Sometimes I dine with my neighbours and friends, and often invite them. My table is neat and well laid, no stinting. I have no taste for gossip, nor do I allow it in my presence. I don't pry into my neighbours' lives, nor watch others with lynx eyes. I hear mass every day; I share what I have with the poor, making no display of good works, so as not to let hypocrisy and vainglory — those enemies that quietly take possession even of the most watchful heart — find an opening into mine. I try to make peace between people I know to be at odds. I am a devoted servant of Our Lady, and my trust is always in the infinite mercy of God our Lord."

Sancho listened with rapt attention to this account of the gentleman's life and pastimes. Thinking it a good, holy life — one whose practitioner ought to be working miracles — he flung himself off Dapple, hurried over, seized the man's right stirrup, and kissed his foot again and again with a devout heart and almost in tears.
Seeing this, the gentleman asked, "What are you doing, brother? What are these kisses for?"
"Let me kiss," said Sancho, "because your worship is the first saint in the saddle I've ever seen in all the days of my life."
"I am no saint," the gentleman replied, "but a great sinner. You, brother, must be the good one — a decent fellow, as your simplicity shows."

Sancho went back and climbed onto his pack-saddle, having coaxed a laugh out of his master's deep melancholy and stirred fresh amazement in Don Diego. Don Quixote then asked him how many children he had, observing that one of the things in which the ancient philosophers — lacking the true knowledge of God — had placed the _summum bonum_ was in the gifts of nature, the gifts of fortune, and in having many friends and many good children.

"Señor Don Quixote," the gentleman answered, "I have one son. Without him, perhaps, I'd count myself happier than I am — not because he's a bad son, but because he isn't as good as I could wish. He is eighteen. He's spent six years at Salamanca studying Latin and Greek, and when I wanted him to move on to the other sciences I found him so wrapped up in poetry (if that can be called a science) that there's no getting him to take to law, which I wanted him to study, or to theology, the queen of them all. I would like him to be an honour to his family, as we live in days when our kings reward learning that is virtuous and worthy, since learning without virtue is a pearl on a dunghill. He spends the whole day deciding whether Homer phrased a particular line of the Iliad correctly, whether Martial was indecent in some epigram, whether such-and-such lines of Virgil are to be understood this way or that — in short, all his talk is of the works of those poets, and of Horace, Persius, Juvenal, and Tibullus. He has little time for modern poets in our own language; and yet, for all his apparent indifference to Spanish verse, his thoughts are absorbed just now in writing a gloss on four lines sent to him from Salamanca, which I suspect are for some poetry contest."

Don Quixote replied to all this: "Children, señor, are portions of their parents' own bowels, and so, whether good or bad, must be loved as we love the souls that give us life. It is for the parents to guide them from infancy in the ways of virtue, propriety, and good Christian conduct, so that grown up they may be the staff of their parents' old age and the glory of their posterity. To force them to study this or that science I don't think wise, though there's no harm in persuading them. And when there's no need to study _pane lucrando_ — when the student is fortunate enough to have parents who provide for him — my advice would be to let him pursue whichever science he seems most drawn to. Poetry may be less useful than pleasurable, but it isn't one of those that bring discredit on its possessor. Poetry, kind sir, is, as I see it, like a tender young maiden of supreme beauty, whom several other maidens — all the rest of the sciences — must array, adorn, and embellish. She has to draw on the help of all of them, and all of them get their lustre from her. But this maiden won't be handled, dragged through the streets, or exposed at the corners of marketplaces or in the closets of palaces. She is the product of an Alchemy of such virtue that whoever knows how to practise it will turn her into pure gold of inestimable worth. He who possesses her must keep her within bounds, not letting her break out into ribald satires or soulless sonnets. She must not be offered for sale, unless it be in heroic poems, moving tragedies, or sprightly, ingenious comedies. She must not be touched by buffoons, nor by the ignorant crowd that can't understand or appreciate her hidden treasures. And don't suppose, señor, that I apply the term 'crowd' here only to plebeians and the lower orders. Anyone who is ignorant — be he lord or prince — may and should be counted among the crowd. The man who embraces and cultivates poetry under the conditions I have named will become famous, and his name honoured throughout all the civilised nations of the earth. As for your saying, señor, that your son thinks little of Spanish poetry, I am inclined to think he isn't quite right there, for this reason: the great poet Homer didn't write in Latin, because he was Greek; nor did Virgil write in Greek, because he was Latin. In short, all the ancient poets wrote in the language they took in with their mother's milk, and never went searching for foreign ones to express their sublime conceptions. That being so, the practice should in justice extend to all nations: the German poet shouldn't be undervalued for writing in his own tongue, nor the Castilian, nor even the Basque, for writing in his. But I suspect, señor, that your son isn't prejudiced against Spanish poetry as such, but against those poets who are merely Spanish versifiers, with no knowledge of other languages or sciences to adorn and enliven their natural inspiration. And yet even in that he may be wrong, for, on a true view, a poet is born one: the poet by nature comes out of his mother's womb a poet, and following the bent heaven has given him, without the aid of study or art, produces work that proves how truly he spoke who said, '_Est Deus in nobis_,' and so on. At the same time, I say that the natural poet who calls in art to his aid will be a far better poet, and will surpass the man who tries to be a poet relying on his knowledge of art alone. The reason is that art does not surpass nature, but only brings it to perfection. Nature combined with art, and art with nature, will produce a perfect poet. To bring my argument to a close, then, kind sir, let your son go on as his star leads him. Since he is, by the sound of it, so studious — and has already successfully cleared the first step of the sciences, which is languages — with their help he will, by his own efforts, reach the summit of polite letters, which so well becomes an independent gentleman, and adorns, honours, and distinguishes him as much as the mitre does the bishop, or the gown the learned counsellor. If your son writes satires that attack other people's honour, scold him, correct him, and tear them up. But if he composes discourses that rebuke vice in general, in the style of Horace, and with elegance like his, praise him — for it is legitimate for a poet to write against envy and lash the envious in his verse, and the other vices too, provided he doesn't single out individuals. There are, however, poets who, for the sake of a clever malice, would risk being banished to the coast of Pontus. If the poet is pure in morals, he'll be pure in his verses too; the pen is the tongue of the mind, and as the thought conceived there is, so will be the things the pen writes down. And when kings and princes see this marvellous science of poetry in wise, virtuous, and thoughtful subjects, they honour them, value them, exalt them, and even crown them with the leaves of the tree the thunderbolt does not strike — as if to show that those whose brows are honoured with such a crown are not to be assailed by anyone."

The man in the green gaban was astonished at Don Quixote's argument — so much so that he began to abandon his idea that he was crazy. But in the middle of the speech, which wasn't entirely to his taste, Sancho had turned off the road to beg a little milk from some shepherds who were milking their ewes nearby. And just as the gentleman, very pleased, was about to pick up the conversation again, Don Quixote raised his head and saw a cart coming along the road they were on, covered with royal flags. Convinced this had to be some new adventure, he called out loudly to Sancho to come and bring him his helmet. Hearing himself called, Sancho left the shepherds and, prodding Dapple hard, came up to his master — to whom there now fell a terrific and desperate adventure.

title: Part 2, Chapter 17
paragraphs: Which sets out the furthest and highest point the unexampled courage of Don Quixote reached or could reach, together with the happily achieved adventure of the lions

The history tells us that when Don Quixote called out to Sancho to bring him his helmet, Sancho was buying some curds that the shepherds had agreed to sell him. Flustered by his master's great haste, he didn't know what to do with them or what to carry them in. Rather than lose them — he had already paid for them — he thought it best to dump them into his master's helmet, and acting on this bright idea he went to see what his master wanted. As he approached, Don Quixote exclaimed:
"Give me that helmet, my friend, for either I know little of adventures, or what I see over there is one that will, and does, call upon me to arm myself."

Hearing this, the man in the green gaban looked in every direction but could see nothing except a cart coming toward them with two or three small flags, which led him to conclude it must be carrying treasure for the King — and he said so to Don Quixote. Don Quixote, however, wouldn't believe him, always convinced that whatever happened to him had to be adventures and still more adventures. So he replied, "The man who is prepared has his battle half fought. Nothing is lost by my preparing myself, for I know by experience that I have enemies, visible and invisible, and I don't know when, or where, or at what moment, or in what shapes they'll attack me." Then, turning to Sancho, he called for his helmet; and Sancho, having no time to take out the curds, had to hand it over just as it was. Don Quixote took it, and without noticing what was inside thrust it down on his head in hot haste. As the curds were pressed and squeezed, the whey began to run all over his face and beard, at which he was so startled that he cried out to Sancho:

"Sancho, what is this? I think my head is softening, or my brains are melting, or I am sweating from head to foot! If I am sweating, it's not from fear. I'm convinced beyond a doubt that the adventure about to befall me is a terrible one. Give me something to wipe myself with, if you have it, for this great sweat is blinding me."

Sancho held his tongue and handed him a cloth, thanking God at the same time that his master hadn't figured out what was going on. Don Quixote then wiped himself, and took off his helmet to see what was making his head feel so cool. Spotting all that white mush inside, he put it to his nose, and as soon as he smelt it he exclaimed:
"By the life of my lady Dulcinea del Toboso, those are curds you've put in here, you treacherous, impudent, ill-mannered squire!"

To which Sancho replied, with great composure and pretended innocence, "If they're curds, give them to me, your worship, and I'll eat them — or rather let the devil eat them, for it must have been he who put them there. As if I would dare dirty your helmet! You've guessed the offender splendidly! By the light God gives me, it seems I must have enchanters too, who persecute me as a creature and limb of your worship, and they must have put that mess there to provoke your patience to anger and make you whack my ribs the way you tend to. Well, this time they have missed their mark, because I trust my master's good sense to see that I have no curds or milk, or anything of the sort; and if I did, it's in my stomach I'd put it, not in the helmet."

"That may be so," said Don Quixote. The gentleman was watching all this with astonishment, especially when, having cleaned himself, his head, face, beard, and helmet, Don Quixote put the helmet back on, settled firmly in his stirrups, eased his sword in the scabbard, gripped his lance, and cried, "Now come who will — here am I, ready to try conclusions with Satan himself in person!"

By this point the cart with the flags had come up, with nobody on it but the carter on a mule and a man sitting up front. Don Quixote planted himself in front of it and said, "Where are you going, brothers? What cart is this? What have you got in it? What flags are those?"

The carter replied, "The cart is mine. What's in it is a pair of wild caged lions, which the governor of Oran is sending to court as a present to his Majesty. The flags are our lord the King's, to show that what is here is his property."
"And are the lions large?" asked Don Quixote.

"So large," replied the man sitting at the door of the cart, "that larger, or as large, have never crossed from Africa to Spain. I am the keeper, and I've brought others over, but never any like these. They're male and female: the male in that first cage, the female in the one behind. They're hungry now, because they've eaten nothing today, so please stand aside, your worship — we have to hurry to where we're going to feed them."

At this, smiling slightly, Don Quixote exclaimed, "Lion whelps for me! Lion whelps for me, and at this hour! Then, by God, those gentlemen who send them here shall see whether I'm a man to be frightened by lions. Get down, my good fellow, and since you're the keeper, open the cages and turn out those beasts; in the middle of this plain I'll show them who Don Quixote of La Mancha is, in spite of, and in the teeth of, the enchanters who send them to me."
"Well, well," said the gentleman to himself at this; "our worthy knight has shown his true colours. The curds, no doubt, have softened his skull and brought his brains to a head."
At that instant Sancho came up to him, saying, "Señor, for God's sake do something to stop my master, Don Quixote, from tackling these lions; if he does, they'll tear us all to pieces here."
"Is your master really so mad," the gentleman asked, "that you believe and fear he'd take on such fierce animals?"
"He's not mad," said Sancho, "but he is reckless."

"I'll put a stop to it," said the gentleman; and going over to Don Quixote, who was insisting that the keeper open the cages, he said, "Sir knight, knight-errants should attempt adventures that hold out the hope of a successful outcome, not those that withhold it entirely. Courage that crosses into recklessness savours more of madness than of bravery. Besides, these lions are not coming to challenge you, nor do they dream of it; they are being sent as presents to his Majesty, and it would be wrong to stop them or delay their journey."

"Kind sir," Don Quixote replied, "you go mind your tame partridge and your bold ferret, and let each man manage his own business. This is mine, and I know whether these gentlemen the lions come for me or not." Then, turning to the keeper, he exclaimed, "By all that's good, sir scoundrel, if you don't open the cages this very instant, I'll pin you to the cart with this lance."

The carter, seeing the determination of this apparition in armour, said, "Please, your worship, for charity's sake, señor — let me unyoke the mules and put myself in safety along with them before the lions are let out. If they kill them on me, I'm ruined for life; all I own is this cart and mules."
"O man of little faith," Don Quixote replied, "get down and unyoke. You'll soon see you're going to all this trouble for nothing, and could have spared yourself the work."

The carter got down and unyoked the mules at top speed, and the keeper called out at the top of his voice, "I call everyone here to witness that against my will and under compulsion I am opening the cages and letting the lions loose, and that I warn this gentleman he will be accountable for all the harm and mischief these beasts may do, and for my salary and dues as well. You, gentlemen, get yourselves to safety before I open up, for I know they won't do me any harm."

Once more the gentleman tried to talk Don Quixote out of doing such a mad thing, saying it was tempting God to attempt such a folly. Don Quixote replied that he knew what he was about. The gentleman in turn begged him to reflect, since he knew he was under a delusion.
"Well, señor," Don Quixote answered, "if you don't care to be a spectator at this tragedy, as in your view it will be, spur your flea-bitten mare and get yourself to safety."

Hearing this, Sancho with tears in his eyes begged him to give up an enterprise compared to which the windmills, and the awful one of the fulling mills, and in fact every feat he'd attempted in the whole course of his life, were cakes and fancy bread. "Look, señor," said Sancho, "there's no enchantment here, nor anything of the sort. Between the bars and chinks of the cage I have seen the paw of a real lion, and going by that, I figure the lion such a paw belongs to must be bigger than a mountain."

"Fear, at any rate," replied Don Quixote, "will make him look bigger to you than half the world. Pull back, Sancho, and leave me; and if I die here, you know our old pact — you'll go to Dulcinea, and I say no more." To this he added more words that killed any hope of his giving up his insane project. The man in the green gaban would have tried to stop him by force, but he found himself outmatched in arms, and didn't think it prudent to come to blows with a madman — which is what Don Quixote had now shown himself to be in every respect. Don Quixote, repeating his orders to the keeper and his threats, warned the gentleman to spur his mare, Sancho his Dapple, and the carter his mules, all striving to get as far from the cart as they could before the lions broke loose. Sancho was weeping over his master's death, for this time he firmly believed it was in store for him from the lions' claws. He cursed his fate, and called it an unlucky hour when he'd thought of taking service with him again. But with all his tears and lamentations he did not forget to thrash Dapple so as to put a good distance between himself and the cart. The keeper, seeing the fugitives were now some way off, once more pleaded and warned as before; but Don Quixote replied that he'd heard him, and he needn't trouble himself with any further warnings or pleas, as they'd be useless, and told him to hurry up.

During the delay while the keeper was opening the first cage, Don Quixote was considering whether it would be better to fight on foot rather than on horseback. He finally decided to fight on foot, afraid that Rocinante might take fright at the sight of the lions. So he sprang off his horse, flung his lance aside, braced his buckler on his arm, drew his sword, and advanced slowly with marvellous intrepidity and resolute courage, to plant himself in front of the cart, commending himself with all his heart to God and to his lady Dulcinea.

It is worth noting that when the author of this truthful history comes to this passage he breaks out into exclamations: "O doughty Don Quixote! Of a spirit beyond all praise! Mirror in which all the heroes of the world may see themselves! Second modern Don Manuel de León, once the glory and honour of Spanish knighthood! In what words shall I describe this dread exploit, by what language shall I make it credible to the ages to come, what eulogies are not deserved by you, even hyperbole piled on hyperbole? On foot, alone, undaunted, high-souled, with only a simple sword — and that no trenchant blade of the Perrillo brand — a shield, but no bright polished steel one, there you stood, biding and awaiting the two fiercest lions Africa's forests ever bred! Let your own deeds be your praise, valiant Manchegan; and here I leave them as they stand, lacking the words to glorify them!"

Here the author's outburst ended, and he took up the thread of his story again, saying that the keeper, seeing that Don Quixote had taken up his position and that it was impossible to avoid letting out the male without incurring the enmity of the fiery and daring knight, flung open the doors of the first cage. It contained, as has been said, the lion, who was now seen to be of enormous size, with a grim and hideous look. The first thing he did was turn around in the cage where he lay, stretch out his claws, and have a thorough stretch. Then he opened his mouth and yawned very leisurely, and with nearly two palms' length of tongue protruding he licked the dust out of his eyes and washed his face. That done, he stuck his head out of the cage and looked all around with eyes like glowing coals — a sight and bearing to strike terror into temerity itself. Don Quixote merely watched him steadily, longing for him to leap from the cart and come to close quarters, where he hoped to hew him in pieces.

So far did his unparalleled madness go. But the noble lion, more courteous than arrogant, paying no attention to silly bravado, after having looked all around as has been said, turned and presented his hindquarters to Don Quixote, and very coolly and tranquilly lay down again in the cage. Seeing this, Don Quixote ordered the keeper to take a stick to him and provoke him so he'd come out.

"That I won't," said the keeper. "If I anger him, the first one he'll tear in pieces will be me. Be satisfied, sir knight, with what you've done — there's nothing more to be said on the score of courage — and don't try to tempt fortune a second time. The lion has the door open; he's free to come out or not. Since he hasn't come out so far, he won't come out today. Your worship's great courage has already been fully demonstrated. No brave champion, as I see it, is bound to do more than challenge his enemy and wait for him on the field. If his opponent doesn't come, the disgrace falls on him, and the one who waits carries off the crown of victory."

"That is true," said Don Quixote. "Close the door, my friend, and give me, in the best form you can, a certificate of what you've seen me do — to wit, that you opened the cage for the lion, that I waited for him, that he didn't come out, that I still waited, and that still he didn't come out and lay down again. I am bound to do no more. Enchantments be gone, and God uphold the right, the truth, and true chivalry! Close the door as I told you, while I make signals to the fugitives who left us, so they may learn this exploit from your lips."

The keeper obeyed, and Don Quixote, fixing on the point of his lance the cloth he had wiped his face with after the deluge of curds, set about recalling the others, who were still in flight, looking back at every step, all in a body, the gentleman bringing up the rear. Sancho, however, happened to notice the signal of the white cloth and exclaimed, "May I die if my master hasn't beaten the wild beasts, for he's calling us back."

They all stopped, and saw that it was Don Quixote making signals. Shaking off their fears somewhat, they approached slowly until they were close enough to hear Don Quixote's voice clearly calling them. At last they returned to the cart, and as they came up, Don Quixote said to the carter, "Hitch up your mules again, brother, and continue your journey. And you, Sancho, give him two gold crowns for himself and the keeper, to make up for the delay they've had on my account."
"That I'll give with all my heart," said Sancho; "but what has become of the lions? Are they dead or alive?"

The keeper then described the end of the contest in full detail, bit by bit, exalting as best he could the valour of Don Quixote, at the sight of whom the lion had quailed and would not — dared not — come out of the cage, although he had held the door open all that time; and how, because he had pointed out to the knight that it was tempting God to provoke the lion to force him out (which the knight wanted done), he had very reluctantly, against his will, allowed the door to be closed.

"What do you think of this, Sancho?" said Don Quixote. "Are there any enchantments that can prevail against true valour? The enchanters may be able to rob me of good fortune, but they can't rob me of fortitude and courage."

Sancho paid the crowns, the carter hitched up, the keeper kissed Don Quixote's hands for the bounty bestowed on him, and promised to give an account of the valiant exploit to the King himself as soon as he saw him at court.

"Then," said Don Quixote, "if his Majesty should happen to ask who performed it, you must say THE KNIGHT OF THE LIONS — for it is my wish that the name I have so far borne of Knight of the Rueful Countenance be from this time forward changed, altered, transformed, and turned into this one. In this I follow the ancient practice of knight-errants, who changed their names whenever they pleased, or whenever it suited their purpose."

The cart went its way, and Don Quixote, Sancho, and the man in the green gaban went theirs. All this time, Don Diego de Miranda hadn't said a word, entirely taken up with watching and noting everything Don Quixote did and said; and the opinion he formed was that he was a man of brains gone mad, and a madman on the verge of rationality. The first part of his history had not yet reached him; had he read it, the amazement at his words and deeds would have vanished, as he would have understood the nature of his madness. But knowing nothing of it, he took him to be rational one moment and crazy the next, since what he said was sensible, elegant, and well expressed, and what he did was absurd, rash, and foolish. And he said to himself, "What could be madder than putting on a helmet full of curds, and then persuading yourself that enchanters are softening your skull? What could be greater rashness and folly than wanting to fight lions tooth and nail?"

Don Quixote roused him from these reflections and this inner monologue by saying, "No doubt, Señor Don Diego de Miranda, you set me down in your own mind as a fool and a madman, and it would be no wonder if you did, since my deeds don't suggest anything else. But for all that, I'd have you take note that I am neither so mad nor so foolish as I must have seemed to you. A gallant knight shows to advantage when he handles his lance deftly against a fierce bull, before the eyes of his sovereign, in the middle of a spacious plaza. A knight shows to advantage clad in glittering armour, pacing the lists before the ladies in some joyous tournament; and all those knights show to advantage who entertain, divert, and — if we may say so — honour the courts of their princes by martial exercises, or what resemble them. But to greater advantage than all these does a knight-errant show, when he travels deserts, lonely places, crossroads, forests, and mountains in quest of perilous adventures, bent on bringing them to a happy and successful end, all to win lasting and glorious renown. To greater advantage, I maintain, does the knight-errant show, bringing aid to some widow in some lonely waste, than the court knight dallying with some city damsel. All knights have their own special parts to play: let the courtier devote himself to the ladies, add lustre to his sovereign's court with his liveries, entertain poor gentlemen with the sumptuous fare of his table, arrange joustings, marshal tournaments, prove himself noble, generous, and magnificent, and above all a good Christian, and so doing he'll fulfil the duties especially his. But let the knight-errant explore the corners of the earth and penetrate the most intricate labyrinths; at every step let him attempt impossibilities; on desolate heaths let him endure the burning rays of the midsummer sun and the bitter cruelty of winter winds and frosts. Let no lions daunt him, no monsters terrify him, no dragons make him quail — for to seek these, to attack those, and to vanquish all are in truth his main duties. I, then, since it has fallen to me to be a member of knight-errantry, can't avoid attempting everything that seems to me to fall within the sphere of my duties. So it was my plain duty to attack those lions just now, although I knew it to be the height of rashness; for I know well what valour is — it is a virtue that occupies a place between two vicious extremes, cowardice and recklessness. But it will be a lesser evil for the valiant man to rise until he reaches recklessness, than to sink until he reaches cowardice. Just as it is easier for the prodigal than for the miser to become generous, so it is easier for a reckless man to prove truly valiant than for a coward to rise to true valour. And believe me, Señor Don Diego, in attempting adventures it is better to lose by a card too many than by a card too few. To hear it said, 'such a knight is rash and daring,' sounds better than 'such a knight is timid and cowardly.'"

"I admit, Señor Don Quixote," said Don Diego, "everything you've said and done is proved correct by the test of reason itself. And I believe that if the laws and ordinances of knight-errantry should be lost, they might be found in your worship's breast as in their own proper depository and archive. But let us hurry on and reach my village, where you can rest after your recent exertions — for if they haven't been of the body, they have been of the spirit, and these sometimes produce bodily fatigue."

"I take the invitation as a great favour and honour, Señor Don Diego," replied Don Quixote; and pressing on at a better pace than before, at about two in the afternoon they reached the village and the house of Don Diego, or, as Don Quixote called him, "The Knight of the Green Gaban."

title: Part 2, Chapter 18
paragraphs: About what happened to Don Quixote in the castle or house of the Knight of the Green Gaban, together with other matters out of the common

Don Quixote found Don Diego de Miranda's house built in village style, with the family arms in rough stone over the street door; in the patio was the storeroom, and at the entrance the cellar, with plenty of wine-jars standing about. These, coming from El Toboso, brought back to his memory his enchanted and transformed Dulcinea; and with a sigh, not thinking what he was saying or in whose presence he was, he exclaimed —
"O ye sweet treasures, to my sorrow found! Once sweet and welcome when heaven willed it so.
"O ye Tobosan jars, how you bring back to mind the sweet object of my bitter regrets!"

The student poet, Don Diego's son, who had come out with his mother to receive him, heard this exclamation, and both mother and son were astonished at the extraordinary figure he cut. He, however, dismounting from Rocinante, advanced with great politeness to ask permission to kiss the lady's hand, while Don Diego said, "Señora, please receive with your usual kindness Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, whom you see before you — a knight-errant, and the bravest and wisest in the world."

The lady, whose name was Doña Cristina, received him with every sign of goodwill and great courtesy, and Don Quixote placed himself at her service in an abundance of well-chosen and polished phrases. Almost the same civilities were exchanged between him and the student, who, listening to Don Quixote, took him to be a sensible, clear-headed man.

Here the author describes minutely everything belonging to Don Diego's mansion, putting before us in his picture the whole contents of a rich gentleman-farmer's house. But the translator of the history thought it best to pass over these and other details of the same sort in silence, as they aren't in keeping with the main purpose of the story, whose strong point is truth rather than dull digressions.

They led Don Quixote into a room, where Sancho removed his armour, leaving him in loose Walloon breeches and a chamois-leather doublet, all stained with the rust of his armour. His collar was a falling one of scholastic cut, without starch or lace; his buskins buff-coloured, his shoes polished. He wore his good sword, hung from a baldric of sea-wolf's skin, for he had suffered for many years, they say, from an ailment of the kidneys; and over it all he threw a long cloak of good grey cloth. But first, with five or six buckets of water (the exact number is disputed), he washed his head and face, and even then the water remained whey-coloured, thanks to Sancho's greed and his purchase of those unlucky curds that had turned his master so white. Thus arrayed, and with an easy, sprightly, gallant air, Don Quixote passed into another room, where the student was waiting to entertain him while the table was being laid. On the arrival of so distinguished a guest, Doña Cristina was anxious to show she knew how, and was able, to give a fitting reception to those who came to her house.

While Don Quixote was taking off his armour, Don Lorenzo (for that was Don Diego's son's name) seized the chance to say to his father, "What are we to make of this gentleman you've brought home, sir? His name, his appearance, and your describing him as a knight-errant have my mother and me completely puzzled."

"I don't know what to say, my son," Don Diego replied. "All I can tell you is that I have seen him perform the acts of the greatest madman in the world, and heard him make observations so sensible that they cancel out everything he does. You talk to him and feel the pulse of his wits, and as you are shrewd, draw the most reasonable conclusion you can about his wisdom or folly — though, to tell the truth, I am more inclined to take him to be mad than sane."

With this, Don Lorenzo went off to entertain Don Quixote as has been said, and in the course of their conversation, Don Quixote said to Don Lorenzo, "Your father, Señor Don Diego de Miranda, has told me of the rare abilities and subtle intellect you have, and, above all, that you are a great poet."

"A poet, perhaps," Don Lorenzo replied, "but a great one, by no means. It's true I am somewhat given to poetry and to reading good poets, but not enough to justify the title of 'great' my father gives me."
"I don't dislike that modesty," said Don Quixote; "for there is no poet who isn't conceited and doesn't think he's the best poet in the world."
"There is no rule without an exception," said Don Lorenzo; "there may be some who are poets and don't think they are."

"Very few," said Don Quixote; "but tell me, what verses are these you have in hand, the ones your father tells me keep you somewhat restless and absorbed? If it's some gloss, I know something about glosses, and I'd like to hear them; and if they're for a poetry contest, try to carry off the second prize — first always goes by favour or personal standing, second by simple justice; so the third comes to be second, and the first, reckoned this way, comes to be third, much as licentiate degrees are awarded at the universities. But for all that, the title of first is a great distinction."
"So far," said Don Lorenzo to himself, "I shouldn't take you for a madman; but let's go on." So he said to him, "You appear to have attended the schools; what sciences have you studied?"
"That of knight-errantry," said Don Quixote, "which is as good as that of poetry, and even a finger or two above it."
"I don't know what science that is," said Don Lorenzo, "and until now I have never heard of it."

"It is a science," said Don Quixote, "that comprehends in itself all or most of the sciences in the world. He who professes it must be a jurist, and must know the rules of justice, distributive and equitable, so as to give each one what belongs to him and is due to him. He must be a theologian, so as to be able to give a clear and distinctive reason for the Christian faith he professes, whenever it is asked of him. He must be a physician, and above all a herbalist, so that in wastes and solitudes he may know the herbs that have the property of healing wounds — a knight-errant can't go searching for someone to cure him at every step. He must be an astronomer, so as to know by the stars how many hours of the night have passed, and what region and quarter of the world he is in. He must know mathematics, for at every turn occasion for them will arise. And, leaving aside that he must be adorned with all the virtues, cardinal and theological, to come down to minor particulars, he must, I say, be able to swim as well as Nicholas or Nicolao the Fish, as the story goes; he must know how to shoe a horse, repair his saddle and bridle; and, to return to higher matters, he must be faithful to God and to his lady; he must be pure in thought, decorous in words, generous in works, valiant in deeds, patient in suffering, compassionate toward the needy, and, lastly, an upholder of the truth, even if defending it should cost him his life. Of all these qualities, great and small, a true knight-errant is made up; judge then, Señor Don Lorenzo, whether it is a contemptible science the knight who studies and professes it has to learn, and whether it may not compare with the very loftiest taught in the schools."
"If that be so," Don Lorenzo replied, "this science, I declare, surpasses them all."
"How, 'if that be so'?" said Don Quixote.
"What I mean to say," said Don Lorenzo, "is that I doubt whether there are now, or ever were, any knight-errants adorned with such virtues."

"Many a time," replied Don Quixote, "have I said what I now say again: that most of the world is of the opinion there never were any knight-errants in it. As it's my view that, unless heaven by some miracle brings home to them the truth that there were and are, all the pains one takes will be wasted (as experience has often shown me), I will not now stop to disabuse you of the error you share with the multitude. All I'll do is pray heaven to deliver you from it, and show you how beneficial and necessary knight-errants were in days of old, and how useful they would be in these days, were they but in fashion. But now, for the sins of the people, sloth and indolence, gluttony and luxury are triumphant."
"Our guest has broken out on our hands," said Don Lorenzo to himself at this point; "but for all that, he is a glorious madman, and I should be a dull blockhead to doubt it."

Here, being called to dinner, they brought their conversation to a close. Don Diego asked his son what he had been able to make out about their guest's wits. To which he replied, "All the doctors and clever scribes in the world won't make sense of the scrawl of his madness; he is a madman full of streaks, full of lucid intervals."

They went in to dinner, and the meal was just what Don Diego had said on the road he was in the habit of giving his guests — neat, plentiful, and tasty. But what pleased Don Quixote most was the marvellous silence that reigned throughout the house, which was like a Carthusian monastery.

When the cloth had been removed, grace said, and their hands washed, Don Quixote earnestly pressed Don Lorenzo to recite the verses for the poetry contest, to which he replied, "Not to be like those poets who refuse when they're asked to recite their verses and vomit them up when they're not, I'll repeat my gloss, for which I don't expect any prize, having composed it merely as an exercise in ingenuity."

"A discerning friend of mine," said Don Quixote, "was of the opinion that no one should waste effort glossing verses. His reason was that the gloss can never live up to the text, and that often — most often — it wanders away from the meaning and purpose of the lines being glossed. Besides, the laws of the gloss are too strict: they allow no questions, no 'said he' or 'I say,' no turning verbs into nouns, no altering the construction, not to mention other restrictions and limitations that fetter gloss-writers, as you no doubt know."
"Really, Señor Don Quixote," said Don Lorenzo, "I wish I could catch your worship tripping at full stretch, but I cannot — you slip through my fingers like an eel."
"I don't understand what you mean by 'slipping,'" said Don Quixote.
"I'll explain another time," said Don Lorenzo; "for the moment, please attend to the glossed verses and the gloss, which run as follows:
Could 'was' become an 'is' for me, / Then would I ask no more than this; / Or could, for me, the time that is / Become the time that is to be! —
GLOSS

Dame Fortune once upon a day / To me was bountiful and kind; / But all things change; she changed her mind, / And what she gave she took away. / O Fortune, long I've sued to thee; / The gifts thou gavest me restore, / For, trust me, I would ask no more, / Could 'was' become an 'is' for me.

No other prize I seek to gain, / No triumph, glory, or success, / Only the long-lost happiness, / The memory whereof is pain. / One taste, methinks, of bygone bliss / The heart-consuming fire might stay; / And, so it come without delay, / Then would I ask no more than this.

I ask what cannot be, alas! / That time should ever be, and then / Come back to us, and be again, / No power on earth can bring to pass; / For fleet of foot is he, I wis, / And idly, therefore, do we pray / That what for aye hath left us may / Become for us the time that is.

Perplexed, uncertain, to remain / 'Twixt hope and fear, is death, not life; / 'Twere better, sure, to end the strife, / And dying, seek release from pain. / And yet, thought were the best for me. / Anon the thought aside I fling, / And to the present fondly cling, / And dread the time that is to be."

When Don Lorenzo had finished reciting his gloss, Don Quixote stood up, and in a loud voice — almost a shout — exclaimed as he grasped Don Lorenzo's right hand in his, "By the highest heavens, noble youth, you are the best poet on earth, and deserve to be crowned with laurel — not by Cyprus or by Gaeta, as a certain poet, God forgive him, said, but by the Academies of Athens, if they still flourished, and by those that flourish now, Paris, Bologna, Salamanca. Heaven grant that the judges who rob you of the first prize — may Phœbus pierce them with his arrows, and the Muses never cross the thresholds of their doors. Recite me some of your long-measure verses, señor, if you would be so good, for I want to feel the pulse of your rare genius thoroughly."

Is there any need to say that Don Lorenzo enjoyed hearing himself praised by Don Quixote, even though he looked on him as a madman? Power of flattery, how far-reaching you are, and how wide are the bounds of your pleasant jurisdiction! Don Lorenzo gave proof of it, for he agreed to Don Quixote's request and recited to him this sonnet on the fable or story of Pyramus and Thisbe.
SONNET

The lovely maid, she pierces now the wall; / Heart-pierced by her young Pyramus doth lie; / And Love spreads wing from Cyprus isle to fly, / A chink to view so wondrous great and small. / There silence speaketh, for no voice at all / Can pass so strait a strait; but love will ply / Where to all other power 'twere vain to try; / For love will find a way whate'er befall. / Impatient of delay, with reckless pace / The rash maid wins the fatal spot where she / Sinks not in lover's arms but death's embrace. / So runs the strange tale, how the lovers twain / One sword, one sepulchre, one memory, / Slays, and entombs, and brings to life again.

"Blessed be God," said Don Quixote when he had heard Don Lorenzo's sonnet, "that among the hosts of irritable poets I have found one consummate one — which, señor, the artistry of this sonnet proves to me that you are!"

For four days Don Quixote was most lavishly entertained at Don Diego's house, at the end of which he asked his permission to leave, telling him he was grateful for the kindness and hospitality he had received there, but that, since it didn't suit knight-errants to give themselves up for long to idleness and luxury, he was eager to fulfil the duties of his calling by seeking adventures, of which he was told there were plenty in that neighbourhood, where he hoped to occupy his time until the day came round for the jousts at Saragossa, which was his proper destination. First of all, he meant to enter the cave of Montesinos, of which so many marvellous things were reported all through the country, and at the same time to investigate and explore the origin and true source of the seven lakes commonly called the lakes of Ruidera.

Don Diego and his son praised his commendable resolution, and told him to take from their house and belongings whatever he wanted, as they would most gladly be of service to him — which indeed his personal worth and his honourable profession made incumbent on them.

The day of his departure came at last, as welcome to Don Quixote as it was sad and sorrowful to Sancho Panza, who was very well satisfied with the abundance of Don Diego's house, and objected to returning to the starvation of the woods and wilds and the short rations of his ill-stocked alforjas. These, however, he filled and packed with what he considered necessary. On taking leave, Don Quixote said to Don Lorenzo, "I don't know if I have told you already, but if I have I'll tell you again: if you want to spare yourself fatigue and toil in reaching the inaccessible summit of the temple of fame, you have only to step off the somewhat narrow path of poetry and take the still narrower one of knight-errantry — wide enough, however, to make you an emperor in the twinkling of an eye."

In this speech Don Quixote wrapped up the evidence of his madness, but even better in what he added when he said, "God knows, I would gladly take Don Lorenzo with me, to teach him how to spare the humble and trample the proud underfoot — virtues that are part and parcel of the profession I belong to. But since his tender age does not allow it, and his praiseworthy pursuits do not permit it, I'll simply content myself with impressing on your worship that you'll become famous as a poet if you are guided by the opinion of others rather than by your own. For no fathers or mothers ever think their own children ugly, and this kind of deception prevails still more strongly in the case of the children of the brain."

Father and son were amazed afresh at the strange medley Don Quixote talked, at one moment sense, at another nonsense, and at the pertinacity and persistence he showed in going through thick and thin in quest of his unlucky adventures, which he made the end and aim of his desires. There was a renewal of offers of service and civilities, and then, with the gracious permission of the lady of the castle, they took their leave — Don Quixote on Rocinante, Sancho on Dapple.

title: Part 2, Chapter 19
paragraphs: In which is told the adventure of the lovesick shepherd, together with other truly droll incidents

Don Quixote had gone only a short distance beyond Don Diego's village when he ran into a couple of either priests or students, and a couple of peasants, mounted on four asses. One of the students carried, wrapped up in a piece of green buckram by way of a portmanteau, what seemed to be a little linen and a couple of pairs of ribbed stockings; the other carried nothing but a pair of new fencing-foils with buttons. The peasants carried various articles that showed they were on their way home from some large town where they had bought them. Both students and peasants were struck with the same amazement everyone felt who saw Don Quixote for the first time, and were dying to know who this man, so different from ordinary men, could be. Don Quixote greeted them, and after finding out that their road was the same as his, offered them his company, asking them to slacken their pace, as their young asses travelled faster than his horse. To oblige them, he told them in a few words who he was and the calling and profession he followed — that of a knight-errant seeking adventures in all parts of the world. He informed them that his own name was Don Quixote of La Mancha, and that he was called, by way of surname, the Knight of the Lions.

All this was Greek or gibberish to the peasants, but not to the students, who very soon spotted the crack in Don Quixote's pate. For all that, they regarded him with admiration and respect, and one of them said to him, "If you, sir knight, have no fixed road — as is the way with those who seek adventures — let your worship come with us. You'll see one of the finest and richest weddings ever celebrated to this day in La Mancha, or for many a league around."

Don Quixote asked if it was some prince's, that he spoke of it in such terms. "Not at all," said the student. "It's the wedding of a farmer and a farmer's daughter — he the richest in all this country, she the fairest mortal ever set eyes on. The display will be something rare and out of the ordinary, because it's to be held in a meadow next to the bride's town. She is called, _par excellence_, Quiteria the fair; the bridegroom is called Camacho the rich. She is eighteen, he twenty-two, and they are fairly matched, though some knowing types — who carry every pedigree in the world by heart — insist that the family of fair Quiteria is better than Camacho's; but nobody minds that nowadays, since wealth can solder a great many flaws. At any rate, Camacho is open-handed, and it's his fancy to roof in the whole meadow with branches, so the sun will have hard work getting in to reach the grass on the ground. He has provided dancers too — not just sword-dancers but also bell-dancers, for in his own town there are people who ring the changes and jingle the bells to perfection. Of shoe-dancers I say nothing, because of those he has hired a host. But none of these things, nor of the many others I've left out, will do more to make this a memorable wedding than the part I suspect the despairing Basilio will play in it. This Basilio is a young man of the same village as Quiteria, and he lived in the house next door to her parents — a circumstance Love seized on to reproduce, to the letter, the long-forgotten loves of Pyramus and Thisbe. Basilio loved Quiteria from his earliest years, and she answered his passion with countless modest tokens of affection, so the loves of the two children, Basilio and Quiteria, were the talk and amusement of the town. As they grew up, Quiteria's father decided to refuse Basilio his usual freedom of access to the house, and to spare himself constant doubts and suspicions, he arranged a match for his daughter with the rich Camacho, not approving of marrying her to Basilio, who had less of fortune's gifts than of nature's. To tell the truth ungrudgingly, Basilio is the most agile youth we know — a mighty thrower of the bar, a first-rate wrestler, a great ball-player. He runs like a deer, leaps better than a goat, knocks down the ninepins as if by magic, sings like a lark, plays the guitar so as to make it speak, and above all handles a sword as well as the best."

"For that excellence alone," Don Quixote put in, "the young man deserves to marry not merely the fair Quiteria, but Queen Guinevere herself, were she alive now, in spite of Lancelot and all who would try to prevent it."

"Say that to my wife," said Sancho, who had until now listened in silence, "because she won't hear of anything but each one marrying his equal, holding with the proverb 'each ewe to her like.' What I would like is for this good Basilio (for I'm beginning to take a fancy to him already) to marry this lady Quiteria. And a blessing and good luck — I meant to say the opposite — on people who would stop those who love one another from marrying."

"If everyone who loved one another were to marry," said Don Quixote, "it would deprive parents of the right to choose, and to marry their children to the proper person at the proper time. If daughters were left to choose husbands as they pleased, one would be for choosing her father's servant, and another some fellow she's seen passing in the street and fancies gallant and dashing, even if he's a drunken bully; for love and infatuation easily blind the eyes of judgment, which are so much needed in choosing one's way of life. The choice of a spouse is very liable to error, and it needs great caution and the special favour of heaven to make it a good one. A man who has to make a long journey, if he is wise, will look for some trusty and pleasant companion to go with him before he sets out. Why, then, should he not do the same who has to make the whole journey of life down to the final halting-place of death — especially when the companion has to be his companion in bed, at the table, and everywhere, as the wife is to her husband? The companionship of one's wife is no article of merchandise that, once bought, may be returned, bartered, or exchanged. It is an inseparable accident that lasts as long as life. It is a noose that, once put round your neck, turns into a Gordian knot, which, if the scythe of Death does not cut it, there is no untying. I could say a great deal more on this subject, were I not held back by the wish to know whether the señor licentiate has anything more to tell about Basilio."

To this the student, bachelor — or, as Don Quixote called him, licentiate — replied, "I have nothing more to say, except that from the moment Basilio learned that fair Quiteria was to marry Camacho the rich, he has never been seen to smile, or heard to utter a rational word. He goes about moody and dejected, talking to himself in a way that shows plainly he is out of his senses. He eats little and sleeps little; all he eats is fruit, and when he sleeps, if he sleeps at all, it is in the field on the bare ground like a brute beast. Sometimes he stares at the sky, at other times he fixes his eyes on the ground in such an abstracted way that he might be taken for a clothed statue, with its drapery stirred by the wind. In short, he shows such signs of a heart crushed by suffering that all of us who know him believe that when fair Quiteria says 'yes' tomorrow, it will be his sentence of death."

"God will guide it better," said Sancho. "God who gives the wound gives the salve; nobody knows what will happen. There are a good many hours between now and tomorrow, and any one of them, or any moment, the house may fall. I have seen the rain coming down and the sun shining at the same time; many a man goes to bed in good health who can't stir the next day. Tell me, is there anyone who can boast of having driven a nail into the wheel of Fortune? No, by my faith. And between a woman's 'yes' and 'no' I wouldn't venture to put the point of a pin — there wouldn't be room for it. If you tell me Quiteria loves Basilio heart and soul, then I'll give him a bag of good luck — for love, I've heard say, looks through spectacles that make copper look like gold, poverty wealth, and bleary eyes pearls."

"What are you driving at, Sancho? Curses on you!" said Don Quixote. "When you take to stringing proverbs and sayings together, nobody can understand you but Judas himself, and I wish he had you. Tell me, you animal, what do you know about nails or wheels or anything else?"

"Oh, if you don't understand me," Sancho replied, "it's no wonder my words are taken for nonsense. But no matter; I understand myself, and I know I haven't said anything very foolish in what I've said — only your worship, señor, is always cavilling at everything I say, indeed everything I do."
"Cavilling, not gravelling," said Don Quixote, "you mangler of honest language — God confound you!"

"Don't find fault with me, your worship," Sancho returned, "for you know I haven't been brought up at court or trained at Salamanca, to know whether I'm adding or dropping a letter in my words. Why, God bless me, it's not fair to force a man from Sayago to speak like a man from Toledo; and maybe there are Toledans who don't hit it off when it comes to polished talk either."

"That is true," said the licentiate, "because those who have been brought up in the Tanneries and the Zocodover can't talk like those who spend nearly all day pacing the cathedral cloisters, and yet they're all Toledans. Pure, correct, elegant, and lucid language will be found in men of courtly breeding and discrimination, even if they were born in Majalahonda. I say of discrimination, because there are many who lack it, and discrimination is the grammar of good language, if accompanied by practice. I, sirs, for my sins, have studied canon law at Salamanca, and I rather pride myself on expressing my meaning in clear, plain, and intelligible language."

"If you didn't pride yourself more on your skill with those foils you carry than on dexterity of tongue," said the other student, "you would have been head of the degrees, where you are now at the tail."
"Look here, bachelor Corchuelo," the licentiate returned, "you have the most mistaken idea in the world about skill with the sword, if you think it useless."

"It's no mere idea on my part, but an established truth," Corchuelo replied. "And if you want me to prove it to you by experiment, you have swords there, and this is a good opportunity. I have a steady hand and a strong arm, and these joined with my resolution, which is not small, will make you admit I am not mistaken. Get down and put your positions and circles and angles and science to work, for I hope to make you see stars at noonday with my rough, raw swordsmanship — in which, next to God, I trust that the man is yet to be born who'll make me turn my back, and that there is no one in the world I won't force to give ground."

"As to whether you turn your back or not, I don't concern myself," the master of fencing replied; "though it might well be that your grave would be dug on the spot where you planted your foot the first time. I mean that you'd be stretched dead there for despising skill with the sword."
"We shall soon see," Corchuelo replied, and getting briskly off his ass he drew out furiously one of the swords the licentiate carried on his beast.

"It mustn't be that way," Don Quixote put in. "I'll be the director of this fencing match, and judge of this often-disputed question." Dismounting from Rocinante and grasping his lance, he planted himself in the middle of the road, just as the licentiate, with an easy, graceful bearing and step, advanced toward Corchuelo, who came on against him darting fire from his eyes, as the saying goes. The other two of the party, the peasants, without dismounting from their asses, served as spectators of the mortal tragedy. The cuts, thrusts, downstrokes, backstrokes, and doubles Corchuelo delivered were past counting, and came faster than hops or hail. He attacked like an angry lion, but was met by a tap on the mouth from the button of the licentiate's sword that checked him in the middle of his furious onset, and made him kiss it as if it were a relic, though not as devoutly as relics are and ought to be kissed. The end of it was that the licentiate counted off for him by thrusts every button on the short cassock he wore, tore the skirts into strips, like the tails of a cuttlefish, knocked off his hat twice, and so completely tired him out that, in vexation, anger, and rage, he took the sword by the hilt and flung it away with such force that one of the peasants there — a notary, who went to retrieve it — afterwards made an affidavit that he had sent it nearly three-quarters of a league; which testimony has served, and serves, to show and establish with full certainty that strength is overcome by skill.

Corchuelo sat down exhausted, and Sancho, approaching, said, "By my faith, señor bachelor, if your worship takes my advice, you'll never challenge anyone to fence again — only to wrestle and throw the bar, for you have the youth and strength for that. But as for these fencers, as they call them, I've heard say they can put the point of a sword through the eye of a needle."

"I'm satisfied with having tumbled off my donkey," said Corchuelo, "and with having had the truth I was so ignorant of proved to me by experience." Getting up, he embraced the licentiate, and they were better friends than ever; and not caring to wait for the notary who had gone for the sword, since they saw he'd be a long time about it, they resolved to push on so as to reach Quiteria's village, where they all belonged, in good time.

During the rest of the journey the licentiate held forth on the excellences of the sword, with such conclusive arguments and such figures and mathematical proofs that all were convinced of the value of the science, and Corchuelo cured of his dogmatism.

It grew dark; but before they reached the town it seemed to all of them as if there was a heaven full of countless glittering stars in front of it. They heard, too, the pleasant mingled notes of a variety of instruments — flutes, drums, psalteries, pipes, tabors, and timbrels — and as they drew near they could see that the trees of a leafy arcade built at the entrance of the town were filled with lights unaffected by the wind, the breeze at the time being so gentle that it had no power to stir the leaves. The musicians were the life of the wedding, wandering through the pleasant grounds in separate bands, some dancing, some singing, others playing the various instruments already mentioned. In short, it seemed as though mirth and merriment were frisking and gambolling all over the meadow. Several other people were busy erecting raised benches from which guests might conveniently watch the plays and dances that were to be performed the next day on the spot dedicated to the celebration of the marriage of Camacho the rich and the obsequies of Basilio. Don Quixote would not enter the village, although both the peasant and the bachelor pressed him; he excused himself, in his own opinion amply, on the grounds that it was the custom of knight-errants to sleep in the fields and woods in preference to towns, even were it under gilded ceilings. So he turned aside a little out of the road, very much against Sancho's will, as the good quarters he had enjoyed in the castle or house of Don Diego came back to his mind.

title: Part 2, Chapter 20
paragraphs: Giving an account of the wedding of Camacho the rich, together with the incident of Basilio the poor

Scarcely had fair Aurora given bright Phœbus time to dry the liquid pearls upon her golden locks with the heat of his fervent rays, when Don Quixote, shaking sloth from his limbs, sprang to his feet and called to his squire Sancho, who was still snoring. Seeing this, Don Quixote, before rousing him, addressed him thus: "Happy you, above all the dwellers on the face of the earth, who, without envying or being envied, sleep with a tranquil mind, and whom neither enchanters persecute nor enchantments frighten. Sleep, I say, and will say a hundred times, with no jealous thoughts of your mistress to make you keep ceaseless vigils, and no cares about how to pay the debts you owe or find tomorrow's food for yourself and your needy little family to interfere with your rest. Ambition does not break your rest, nor does this world's empty pomp disturb you; the utmost reach of your anxiety is to provide for your ass, since upon my shoulders you have laid the support of yourself, the counterweight and burden that nature and custom have imposed on masters. The servant sleeps, and the master lies awake thinking how to feed him, advance him, and reward him. The distress of seeing the sky turn brazen and withhold its needful moisture from the earth is felt not by the servant but by the master, who in times of scarcity and famine must support the one who served him in times of plenty and abundance."

To all this Sancho made no reply, because he was asleep; nor would he have wakened up so soon as he did, had not Don Quixote brought him round with the butt of his lance. He woke at last, drowsy and lazy, and casting his eyes about in every direction, observed, "From the direction of that arcade comes, if I'm not mistaken, a steam and a smell a great deal more like fried rashers than galingale or thyme. A wedding that begins with smells like that, by my faith, ought to be plentiful and unstinting."
"Enough, glutton," said Don Quixote. "Come, let us go and witness this wedding, and see what the rejected Basilio does."

"Let him do what he likes," Sancho returned. "If he weren't poor, he would marry Quiteria. To make a grand match for himself, and he without a farthing — is there nothing else?
