By my faith, señor, it's my view that the poor man should be content with what he can get, and not go looking for dainties at the bottom of the sea. I'll bet my arm that Camacho could bury Basilio in reales; and if that's so, as no doubt it is, what a fool Quiteria would be to refuse the fine dresses and jewels Camacho must have given her and will give her, and take instead Basilio's bar-throwing and swordplay. They won't give a pint of wine at the tavern for a good cast of the bar or a neat thrust of the sword. Talents and accomplishments that can't be turned into money — let Count Dirlos have them. But when such gifts fall on someone with hard cash, I only wish my own station in life were as becoming as those gifts. On a good foundation you can raise a good building, and the best foundation in the world is money."

"For God's sake, Sancho," said Don Quixote here, "stop that harangue. I believe that if you were allowed to go on with everything you start every other minute, you'd have no time left for eating or sleeping; you'd spend it all in talking."

"If your worship had a good memory," Sancho replied, "you'd remember the articles of our agreement before we set out from home this last time. One of them was that I was to be allowed to say all I liked, so long as it was not against my neighbour or your worship's authority; and so far, it seems to me, I have not broken that article."

"I remember no such article, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "and even if it were so, I want you to hold your tongue and come along, for the instruments we heard last night are already starting to enliven the valleys again, and no doubt the marriage will take place in the cool of the morning, and not in the heat of the afternoon."

Sancho did as his master told him, and putting the saddle on Rocinante and the pack-saddle on Dapple, they both mounted and at a leisurely pace entered the arcade. The first thing that met Sancho's eyes was a whole ox spitted on a whole elm tree, and in the fire over which it was to be roasted was burning a middling-sized mountain of faggots. Six stewpots that stood around the blaze had not been made in the ordinary mould of common pots: they were six half wine-jars, each fit to hold the contents of a slaughter-house — they swallowed whole sheep and hid them away inside without showing any more sign of them than if they were pigeons. Countless hares lay ready skinned, and plucked fowls hung from the trees ready for burial in the pots; numberless wildfowl and game of various sorts were suspended from the branches so the air might keep them cool. Sancho counted more than sixty wineskins of over six gallons each, all filled, as proved afterwards, with generous wines. There were also piles of the whitest bread, like the heaps of grain one sees on threshing-floors. There was a wall made of cheeses arranged like open brickwork, and two cauldrons full of oil, bigger than those of a dyer's shop, served for cooking fritters, which when fried were taken out with two mighty shovels and plunged into another cauldron of prepared honey standing close by. Of cooks and cook-maids there were more than fifty, all clean, brisk, and cheerful. In the capacious belly of the ox were a dozen soft little sucking-pigs, which, sewn up there, served to give it tenderness and flavour. The spices of various kinds did not seem to have been bought by the pound but by the quarter, and all lay open to view in a great chest. In short, all the preparations for the wedding were in rustic style, but plentiful enough to feed an army.

Sancho observed all, contemplated all, and everything won his heart. The first to captivate and take his fancy were the pots, out of which he would have very gladly helped himself to a moderate pipkinful; then the wineskins secured his affections; and lastly, the produce of the frying-pans — if indeed such imposing cauldrons can be called frying-pans. Unable to control himself or bear it any longer, he approached one of the busy cooks and civilly but hungrily begged permission to soak a scrap of bread in one of the pots. The cook answered, "Brother, this is not a day on which hunger is to have any sway, thanks to the rich Camacho. Get down and look about for a ladle and skim off a hen or two, and much good may they do you."
"I don't see one," said Sancho.

"Wait a moment," said the cook; "sinner that I am, how particular and shy you are!" So saying, he seized a bucket and plunging it into one of the half-jars took up three hens and a couple of geese, and said to Sancho, "Fall to, friend, and take the edge off your appetite with these skimmings until dinnertime comes."
"I have nothing to put them in," said Sancho.
"Well then," said the cook, "take spoon and all — for Camacho's wealth and happiness furnish everything."

While Sancho was thus occupied, Don Quixote was watching the entrance, at one end of the arcade, of some twelve peasants, all in holiday and gala dress, mounted on twelve beautiful mares with rich, handsome field trappings and a number of little bells attached to their petrals. Marshalled in regular order, they ran not one but several courses over the meadow, with jubilant shouts and cries of "Long live Camacho and Quiteria! He as rich as she is fair, and she the fairest on earth!"
Hearing this, Don Quixote said to himself, "It's easy to see these folk have never seen my Dulcinea del Toboso; for if they had, they'd be more moderate in their praises of this Quiteria of theirs."

Shortly after this, several bands of dancers of various sorts began to enter the arcade at different points, and among them one of sword-dancers, composed of some twenty-four lads of gallant and high-spirited bearing, dressed in the finest and whitest of linen, and with handkerchiefs embroidered in various colours with fine silk. One of those on the mares asked an active youth who led them whether any of the dancers had been wounded. "As yet, thank God, no one has been wounded," he said; "we are all safe and sound." And he at once began to execute complicated figures with the rest of his comrades, with so many turns and so great dexterity that, although Don Quixote was well used to seeing dances of the same kind, he thought he had never seen any so good as this. He also admired another that came in, made up of fair young maidens, none of whom seemed to be under fourteen or over eighteen, all dressed in green stuff, with their hair partly braided, partly flowing loose, but all of such bright gold as to vie with the sunbeams; and over their hair they wore garlands of jasmine, roses, amaranth, and honeysuckle. At their head were a venerable old man and an ancient dame, more brisk and active, however, than might have been expected from their years. The notes of a Zamora bagpipe accompanied them, and with modesty in their faces and in their eyes, and lightness in their feet, they looked the best dancers in the world.

Following these came an artistic dance of the sort they call "speaking dances." It was composed of eight nymphs in two files, with the god Cupid leading one and Interest the other — the former furnished with wings, bow, quiver, and arrows, the latter in a rich dress of gold and silk of various colours. The nymphs who followed Love bore their names written on white parchment in large letters on their backs. "Poetry" was the name of the first, "Wit" of the second, "Birth" of the third, and "Valour" of the fourth. Those who followed Interest were distinguished in the same way: the badge of the first announced "Liberality," that of the second "Largess," the third "Treasure," the fourth "Peaceful Possession." In front of them all came a wooden castle drawn by four wild men, all clad in ivy and hemp dyed green, and looking so lifelike that they nearly terrified Sancho. On the front of the castle and on each of the four sides of its frame it bore the inscription "Castle of Caution." Four skilful tabor and flute players accompanied them, and the dance having been opened, Cupid, after executing two figures, raised his eyes and bent his bow against a damsel who stood between the turrets of the castle, and addressed her thus:

I am the mighty God whose sway / Is potent over land and sea. / The heavens above us own me; nay, / The shades below acknowledge me. / I know not fear, I have my will, / Whate'er my whim or fancy be; / For me there's no impossible, / I order, bind, forbid, set free.

Having concluded the stanza he discharged an arrow at the top of the castle, and went back to his place. Interest then came forward and went through two more figures; and as soon as the tabors ceased, he said:

But mightier than Love am I, / Though Love it be that leads me on, / Than mine no lineage is more high, / Or older, underneath the sun. / To use me rightly few know how, / To act without me fewer still, / For I am Interest, and I vow / For evermore to do thy will.
Interest retired, and Poetry came forward; and when she had gone through her figures like the others, fixing her eyes on the damsel of the castle, she said:

With many a fanciful conceit, / Fair Lady, winsome Poesy / Her soul, an offering at thy feet, / Presents in sonnets unto thee. / If thou my homage wilt not scorn, / Thy fortune, watched by envious eyes, / On wings of poesy upborne / Shall be exalted to the skies.
Poetry withdrew, and on the side of Interest, Liberality advanced; and after going through her figures she said:

To give, while shunning each extreme, / The sparing hand, the over-free, / Therein consists, so wise men deem, / The virtue Liberality. / But thee, fair lady, to enrich, / Myself a prodigal I'll prove, / A vice not wholly shameful, which / May find its fair excuse in love.

In the same manner all the characters of the two bands advanced and retired, and each executed its figures and delivered its verses, some of them graceful, some burlesque; but Don Quixote's memory (although he had an excellent one) only carried away those just quoted. Then all mingled together, forming chains and breaking off again with graceful, unconstrained gaiety; and whenever Love passed in front of the castle he shot his arrows up at it, while Interest broke gilded pellets against it. At length, after they had danced a good while, Interest drew out a great purse, made of the skin of a large brindled cat and to all appearance full of money, and flung it at the castle; and with the force of the blow the boards fell asunder and tumbled down, leaving the damsel exposed and unprotected. Interest and the characters of his band advanced, and throwing a great chain of gold over her neck, pretended to lead her away captive. On seeing this, Love and his supporters made as though they would release her, the whole action being to the accompaniment of the tabors and in the form of a regular dance. The wild men made peace between them, and with great dexterity readjusted and fixed the boards of the castle, and the damsel once more ensconced herself within; and with this the dance wound up, to the great enjoyment of the spectators.

Don Quixote asked one of the nymphs who it was that had composed and arranged it. She replied that it was a beneficiary of the town who had a nice taste in devising things of the sort. "I would lay a wager," said Don Quixote, "that this same bachelor or beneficiary is a greater friend of Camacho's than of Basilio's, and that he is better at satire than at vespers; he has worked the accomplishments of Basilio and the riches of Camacho very neatly into the dance." Sancho Panza, who was listening to all this, exclaimed, "The king is my cock — I stick to Camacho." "It's easy to see you're a peasant, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and one of the sort that cry 'Long life to the conqueror.'"

"I don't know what sort I am," Sancho returned, "but I know very well that I'll never get such elegant skimmings off Basilio's pots as these I've got off Camacho's." And he showed him the bucketful of geese and hens, and seizing one began to eat with great gusto and appetite, saying, "A fig for the accomplishments of Basilio! As much as you have, so much are you worth; and as much as you are worth, so much do you have. As a grandmother of mine used to say, there are only two families in the world, the Haves and the Have-nots; and she stuck to the Haves. And to this day, Señor Don Quixote, people would sooner feel the pulse of 'Have' than of 'Know'; an ass covered with gold looks better than a horse with a pack-saddle. So once more I say I stick to Camacho — whose bountiful pot-skimmings are geese and hens, hares and rabbits — and not to Basilio's, whose, if any ever come to hand, or even to foot, will only be rinsings."

"Have you finished your harangue, Sancho?" said Don Quixote. "Of course I have finished it," Sancho replied, "because I see your worship takes offence at it; but if it weren't for that, there was work enough cut out for three days."
"God grant I may see you dumb before I die, Sancho," said Don Quixote.

"At the rate we are going," said Sancho, "I'll be chewing clay before your worship dies; and then, maybe, I'll be so dumb that I won't say a word until the end of the world, or at least till the day of judgment."

"Even if that happens, O Sancho," said Don Quixote, "your silence will never make up for all you have talked, are talking, and will talk all your life. Besides, it stands to reason that my death will come before yours; so I never expect to see you dumb, not even when you are drinking or sleeping, and that is the utmost I can say."

"In good faith, señor," Sancho replied, "there's no trusting that fleshless one — I mean Death — who devours the lamb as soon as the sheep, and, as I've heard our curate say, treads with equal foot upon the lofty towers of kings and the lowly huts of the poor. That lady is more mighty than dainty; she's in no way squeamish, she devours everything and is ready for everything, and fills her alforjas with people of all sorts, ages, and ranks. She's no reaper that sleeps out the noontide; at all hours she is reaping and cutting down the dry grass as well as the green. She never seems to chew, but bolts and swallows everything put before her, for she has a canine appetite that is never satisfied. And though she has no belly, she shows she has a dropsy and is thirsty to drink the lives of all who live, as one would drink a jug of cold water."

"Say no more, Sancho," said Don Quixote here; "don't try to better it, and risk a fall. In truth, what you have said about death in your rustic phrase is what a good preacher might have said. I tell you, Sancho, if you had discretion to match your native wit, you might take a pulpit in hand, and go about the world preaching fine sermons." "He preaches well who lives well," said Sancho, "and I know no more theology than that."
"Nor need you," said Don Quixote, "but I cannot conceive or make out how it is that, the fear of God being the beginning of wisdom, you, who are more afraid of a lizard than of Him, know so much."

"Pass judgment on your chivalries, señor," Sancho returned, "and don't set yourself up to judge of other men's fears or braveries, for I am as good a fearer of God as my neighbours. But leave me to finish off these skimmings, for all the rest is only idle talk that we'll be called to account for in the other world." And so saying, he began a fresh attack on the bucket with such hearty appetite that he aroused Don Quixote's, who no doubt would have helped him had he not been prevented by what must be told further on.

title: Part 2, Chapter 21
paragraphs: In which Camacho's wedding continues, along with other delightful incidents

While Don Quixote and Sancho were occupied with the conversation recorded in the previous chapter, they heard loud shouting and a great commotion, raised by the men on the mares as they galloped at full speed, yelling, to greet the bride and bridegroom, who were now approaching surrounded by musical instruments and pageantry of every kind, accompanied by the priest, the relatives of both families, and all the most distinguished people of the neighboring villages. The moment Sancho caught sight of the bride, he cried out, “By my faith, she isn’t dressed like a village girl at all, but like some elegant lady of the court. Good heavens, as far as I can tell, the patena she’s wearing is rich coral, and her green Cuenca cloth is thirty-pile velvet—and that white linen trimming, I’ll swear it’s satin! Look at her hands, with jet rings on them! May luck never find me if those aren’t gold rings, real gold too, set with pearls as white as curdled milk, every single one worth an eye out of your head. And what hair the hussy has! If it isn’t a wig, I’ve never seen longer or fairer hair in all my days. See how splendidly she carries herself—and that figure! Wouldn’t you say she’s like a walking palm tree loaded down with clusters of dates? Because the trinkets dangling from her hair and her neck look exactly like them. I swear from my heart she’s a fine, spirited girl, fit ‘to pass over the banks of Flanders.’”

Don Quixote laughed at Sancho’s rustic praise, though he privately thought that, apart from his lady Dulcinea del Toboso, he had never laid eyes on a more beautiful woman. The lovely Quiteria looked somewhat pale, no doubt because of the sleepless night brides always endure getting themselves ready for their wedding the next day. The procession moved toward a stage that stood at one side of the meadow, decorated with carpets and green boughs, where the couple were to exchange their vows and from which they would watch the dances and entertainments. But just as they reached the spot, they heard a loud cry behind them and a voice calling out, “Wait a moment, you people, as thoughtless as you are hasty!” Everyone turned at these words and saw that the speaker was a man dressed in what looked like a loose black coat trimmed with crimson patches shaped like flames. He was crowned, as they soon saw, with a wreath of mournful cypress, and he carried a long staff in his hand. As he drew nearer, everyone recognized him as the gallant Basilio, and they all waited anxiously to see what his words would lead to, fearing some disaster from his arrival at such a moment. He came up at last, exhausted and out of breath, planted himself before the bridal pair, and drove his staff, which had a steel point at its end, into the ground. Then, his face pale and his eyes fixed on Quiteria, he addressed her in a hoarse, trembling voice:

“You know perfectly well, ungrateful Quiteria, that under the holy law we both profess, you can take no other husband while I am alive; nor are you unaware that, while I hoped time and my own labors would mend my fortunes, I never once failed to show the respect your honor deserved. Yet you, throwing aside everything you owe to my faithful love, are about to hand over what belongs to me to another man, whose wealth brings him not merely good fortune but the highest happiness. And now, to crown that happiness—not because I think he deserves it, but because heaven has chosen to grant it to him—I will remove with my own hands the obstacle that might stand in its way, and take myself out from between you. Long live the rich Camacho! May he enjoy many happy years with the ungrateful Quiteria! And let poor Basilio die—Basilio, whose poverty clipped the wings of his happiness and laid him in the grave!”

With these words he seized the staff he had driven into the ground, and, leaving half of it fixed there, revealed that it was a sheath concealing a fairly long rapier. Then, with what might be called its hilt planted in the earth, he threw himself upon it swiftly, coolly, and deliberately, and in an instant the bloody point and half the steel blade emerged from his back, the unfortunate man collapsing to the ground bathed in his own blood and run through by his own weapon.

His friends rushed at once to help him, stricken with grief at his misery and tragic end, and Don Quixote, dismounting from Rocinante, hurried to support him and gathered him into his arms, finding that he had not yet stopped breathing. They were about to pull out the rapier, but the priest standing nearby objected to its being withdrawn before Basilio had made his confession, since the moment it came out would be the moment of his death. Basilio, however, revived a little and said in a faint voice, as though in pain, “If you would only consent, cruel Quiteria, to give me your hand as my bride in this last fatal moment, I might still hope that my recklessness would find pardon, since through it I won the bliss of being yours.”

On hearing this, the priest told him to think about the welfare of his soul rather than the desires of his body, and to beg God in all earnestness for pardon for his sins and for his desperate act; to which Basilio answered that he was resolved not to confess unless Quiteria first gave him her hand in marriage, for that happiness would settle his mind and give him the strength to make his confession.

When Don Quixote heard the wounded man’s plea, he declared loudly that what Basilio asked was fair and reasonable, and what is more, a request easily granted; and that Señor Camacho would gain just as much honor by receiving the lady Quiteria as the widow of the brave Basilio as if he had received her straight from her father’s hands.
“In this case,” he said, “nothing is required but a single ‘yes,’ and no consequences can follow from speaking the word, since the marriage bed of this union must be the grave.”

Camacho listened to all this, perplexed and bewildered, not knowing what to say or do; but the pleas of Basilio’s friends were so insistent—begging him to let Quiteria give Basilio her hand, so that his soul would not be lost by leaving this life in despair—that they persuaded, indeed compelled, him to say that if Quiteria was willing to give it, he was content, since it only delayed the fulfillment of his own wishes by a moment. Immediately they all turned on Quiteria and pressed her—some with prayers, some with tears, others with persuasive arguments—to give her hand to poor Basilio; but she, harder than marble and more unmoved than any statue, seemed unable or unwilling to speak a single word, and she would have given no answer at all had the priest not told her to decide quickly what she meant to do, since Basilio’s soul was now at his teeth and there was no time left for hesitation.

At this the fair Quiteria, looking distressed, grief-stricken, and remorseful, walked without a word to where Basilio lay, his eyes already rolling back, his breathing quick and labored, murmuring Quiteria’s name between his teeth, and seemingly about to die like a heathen rather than a Christian. Quiteria came up to him and, kneeling, asked for his hand by gestures, without speaking. Basilio opened his eyes, gazed steadily at her, and said, “O Quiteria, why have you turned compassionate at the very moment when your compassion will serve as a dagger to take my life? I no longer have the strength either to bear the happiness you give me in accepting me as your own, or to hold back the pain that is fast drawing the dreadful shadow of death across my eyes. What I beg of you, O fatal star of mine, is that the hand you ask of me, and would give me in return, not be offered out of mere politeness or to deceive me once again, but that you confess and declare that you give it freely, without any constraint upon your will, to me as your lawful husband; for it is not right that you should trifle with me at a moment like this, or resort to lies with a man who has always dealt so honestly with you.”

As he spoke these words he grew so faint that the onlookers expected each spell of weakness to carry his life away with it. Then Quiteria, overcome with modesty and shame, took Basilio’s hand in her right hand and said, “No force could ever bend my will; and so, as freely as it is possible for me to do, I give you the hand of a lawful wife, and I take yours, if you give it to me of your own free will, undisturbed and unclouded by the calamity your rash act has brought upon you.”
“Yes, I give it,” said Basilio, “not shaken or confused, but with the clear reason heaven is pleased to grant me; and so I give myself to you to be your husband.”
“And I give myself to be your wife,” said Quiteria, “whether you live for many years or they carry you from my arms to the grave.”

“For a man so badly wounded,” Sancho remarked at this point, “this young fellow has a great deal to say. They ought to make him stop his billing and cooing and attend to his soul; for as far as I can tell, he has it more on his tongue than at his teeth.”

When Basilio and Quiteria had joined hands in this way, the priest, deeply moved and with tears in his eyes, pronounced the blessing over them and prayed that heaven would grant an easy passage to the soul of the newly married man—who, the instant he received the blessing, sprang nimbly to his feet and, with astonishing audacity, pulled out the rapier that had been sheathed in his body. All the bystanders were dumbfounded, and some of them, more simple than curious, began shouting, “A miracle, a miracle!” But Basilio answered, “No miracle, no miracle—just a trick, a trick!” The priest, bewildered and astonished, hurried to examine the wound with both hands and discovered that the blade had passed not through Basilio’s flesh and ribs but through a hollow iron tube filled with blood, which he had cleverly fitted in place; the blood, as was later learned, had been specially prepared so that it would not clot. In short, the priest, Camacho, and most of those present realized they had been tricked and made fools of. The bride showed no sign of resentment at the deception; on the contrary, when she heard people saying that the marriage could not be valid because it had been obtained by fraud, she declared that she confirmed it all over again—from which everyone concluded that the whole affair had been planned with the knowledge and agreement of the pair. Camacho and his supporters were so humiliated by this that they resolved to take their revenge by force, and a great many of them drew their swords and rushed at Basilio, in whose defense almost as many swords were unsheathed in an instant, while Don Quixote, leading the way on horseback with his lance couched over his arm and well covered by his shield, made everyone fall back before him. Sancho, who never found any pleasure or entertainment in affairs of this kind, retreated to the wine-jars from which he had skimmed his delicious froth, judging that such a spot, being holy ground, would be respected.

“Hold, gentlemen, hold!” Don Quixote shouted. “We have no right to take vengeance for the wrongs that love does us. Remember that love and war are one and the same thing; and just as in war it is lawful and customary to use tricks and stratagems to defeat the enemy, so in the contests and rivalries of love the schemes and devices used to reach the desired end are legitimate, provided they bring no discredit or dishonor upon the beloved. Quiteria belonged to Basilio, and Basilio to Quiteria, by the just and kindly ordering of heaven. Camacho is rich and can buy his pleasure when, where, and however he likes. Basilio has only this one ewe-lamb, and no man, however powerful, shall take her from him; these two whom God has joined, no man may put asunder—and whoever attempts it must first get past the point of this lance.” And with that he brandished it so vigorously and so skillfully that he struck fear into everyone who did not know him.

But Quiteria’s rejection had made so deep an impression on Camacho’s mind that it drove her out of his thoughts in an instant; and so the counsel of the priest, a wise and well-meaning man, prevailed with him, and through it he and his partisans were calmed and quieted. To prove it they sheathed their swords again, blaming Quiteria’s pliability rather than Basilio’s cunning; Camacho arguing that if Quiteria had loved Basilio so much as an unmarried girl, she would have gone on loving him as a married woman, and that he ought to thank heaven more for taking her away than for having given her to him.

With Camacho and his followers thus consoled and pacified, Basilio’s party calmed down as well; and the rich Camacho, to show he bore no grudge over the trick and thought nothing of it, asked that the celebration continue exactly as if he had really been married. But neither Basilio nor his bride nor their followers would take any part in it, and they withdrew to Basilio’s village; for the poor, when they are people of virtue and good sense, have those who follow, honor, and stand by them, just as the rich have those who flatter them and dance attendance on them. They took Don Quixote along with them, regarding him as a man of worth and courage. Only Sancho had a cloud over his soul, for he found himself cut off from Camacho’s splendid feast and festivities, which went on until nightfall; and so, dragged away, he trudged gloomily after his master, who rode with Basilio’s party, leaving behind the flesh-pots of Egypt—though he carried them with him in his heart, and the skimmings in his bucket, now nearly gone, conjured up before his eyes visions of the glory and abundance of the good cheer he was losing. And so, annoyed and dejected though not hungry, without ever dismounting from Dapple, he followed in the footsteps of Rocinante.

title: Part 2, Chapter 22
paragraphs: Which relates the grand adventure of the Cave of Montesinos in the heart of La Mancha, which the valiant Don Quixote brought to a happy conclusion

The newly married couple showered Don Quixote with attentions, great and many, feeling deeply indebted to him for stepping forward to defend their cause; and they praised his wisdom as highly as his courage, ranking him a Cid in arms and a Cicero in eloquence. Good Sancho enjoyed himself for three days at the couple's expense, and from them the travelers learned that the fake wound had not been a plot arranged with the fair Quiteria but a scheme of Basilio's own, who had counted on producing exactly the result everyone had witnessed. He did admit, it is true, that he had let a few of his friends in on the idea, so that at the right moment they could back him up and make sure the trick succeeded.

“That,” said Don Quixote, “is not and should not be called deception when it aims at a virtuous end;” and the marriage of two lovers, he insisted, was the most excellent of ends. He reminded them, however, that love has no greater enemy than hunger and constant need, because love is all lightness, pleasure, and happiness—especially when the lover actually possesses the one he loves—and poverty and want are the sworn enemies of all three. He said this to urge Señor Basilio to give up practicing the accomplishments he was so skilled at, since they brought him fame but no money, and to devote himself instead to earning a living by honest industry, which never fails those who are prudent and persistent. The poor man who is a man of honor (if a poor man can truly be one) owns a jewel when he has a beautiful wife, and if she is taken from him, his honor is taken too, and killed. The beautiful woman who guards her honor while her husband is poor deserves to be crowned with the laurels and garlands of victory and triumph. Beauty on its own draws the desire of everyone who sees it, and royal eagles and high-soaring birds swoop down on it as on a tempting lure; but when beauty comes joined to need and poverty, then the ravens and the kites and the other birds of prey attack it as well, and the woman who stands firm against such assaults richly deserves to be called her husband's crown. “Remember, prudent Basilio,” Don Quixote added, “a certain sage—I forget which one—held the opinion that there was only one good woman in the entire world, and his advice was that every man should think and believe that this single good woman was his own wife; that way he would live happily. I myself am not married, and so far the thought of marrying has never crossed my mind; even so, I would venture to advise anyone who asked me how he should go about finding a wife he would be content to marry. The first thing I would recommend is that he look to reputation rather than wealth, for a good woman does not earn a good name merely by being good, but by visibly showing that she is; open looseness and free behavior damage a woman's honor far more than secret vice does. If you bring a good woman into your house, it will be easy to keep her good, and even to make her better; but if you bring in a bad one, you will find it hard work to reform her, because moving from one extreme to the other is no simple matter. I do not say it is impossible; I only consider it difficult.”

Sancho, taking all this in, said to himself, “This master of mine, whenever I say anything with weight and substance to it, tells me I could pick up a pulpit and travel the world preaching fine sermons; but I say of him that once he starts stringing maxims together and handing out advice, he could carry not just one pulpit but two on every finger, and hold forth in the marketplaces to his heart's content. Devil take you for a knight-errant—the things you know! I used to believe, deep down, that the only subject he understood was anything touching his chivalry; but there's nothing he won't stick a finger into.”
Sancho muttered this a bit too loudly, and his master overheard him and asked, “What are you muttering there, Sancho?”

“I'm not saying anything, not muttering anything,” said Sancho; “I was only telling myself I wish I'd heard what your worship just said before I got married; maybe now I'd be saying, ‘The ox that's loose licks himself where he pleases.’”
“Is your Teresa really so bad, Sancho?”
“She's not very bad,” Sancho replied; “but she's not very good either; at least, not as good as I'd like her to be.”

“You do wrong, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “to speak ill of your wife; after all, she is the mother of your children.” “Then we're even,” Sancho answered, “because she speaks ill of me whenever the mood takes her—above all when she's jealous; Satan himself couldn't stand her then.”

In the end they stayed three days with the newlyweds, who entertained and treated them like kings. Don Quixote asked the fencing licentiate to find him a guide who could lead him to the Cave of Montesinos, since he had a great desire to go inside and see with his own eyes whether the marvelous stories told about it all across the region were true. The licentiate said he would get him a cousin of his, a noted scholar with a strong appetite for books of chivalry, who would be delighted to bring him to the very mouth of the cave and would also show him the lakes of Ruidera, famous throughout La Mancha and indeed all of Spain; and he assured him he would find the man good company, for he was a young fellow capable of writing books fit to be printed and dedicated to princes. The cousin arrived at last, leading a she-ass in foal whose pack-saddle was covered with a patchwork carpet or piece of sackcloth; Sancho saddled Rocinante, got Dapple ready, and stocked his alforjas, alongside the cousin's, which were equally well filled; and so, commending themselves to God and saying goodbye to everyone, they set off down the road toward the famous Cave of Montesinos.

Along the way Don Quixote asked the cousin what kind and character of pursuits, occupations, and studies he followed, and the cousin answered that his profession was that of a humanist, and that his work and study consisted of composing books for the press, all of great usefulness and no less entertainment to the nation. One was called “The Book of Liveries,” in which he described seven hundred and three liveries with their colors, mottoes, and ciphers, so that gentlemen of the court could pick out whichever they fancied for festivals and celebrations without having to beg them from anyone or rack their brains, as the saying goes, to make them fit their aims and intentions; “for,” he said, “I supply the jealous, the rejected, the forgotten, and the absent with exactly what suits them, guaranteed to fit. I have another book as well, which I plan to call ‘Metamorphoses, or the Spanish Ovid,’ a work of rare and original invention, for in it, imitating Ovid in a burlesque vein, I reveal who the Giralda of Seville and the Angel of the Magdalena really were, what the sewer of Vecinguerra at Córdoba was, what the bulls of Guisando were, and the Sierra Morena, and the Leganitos and Lavapiés fountains in Madrid, not forgetting those of the Piojo, the Caño Dorado, and the Priora—all with their allegories, metaphors, and transformations, so that the book amuses, interests, and instructs all at once. I have yet another book, which I call ‘The Supplement to Polydore Vergil,’ dealing with the invention of things; it is a work of great learning and research, for I establish and elegantly clarify several matters of real importance that Polydore neglected to mention. He forgot to tell us who was the first man in the world to catch a cold in the head, and who was the first to try salivation as a cure for the French disease; but I set it all down precisely, citing more than twenty-five authors as proof, so you can see I have labored to good purpose and that the book will be of service to the whole world.”

Sancho, who had been listening closely to the cousin's words, said to him, “Tell me, señor—and may God give you luck with the printing of your books—can you tell me (and of course you can, since you know everything) who was the first man ever to scratch his head? To my mind it must have been our father Adam.”
“It must indeed,” replied the cousin; “for there is no doubt Adam had a head and hair on it; and being the first man in the world, he would surely have scratched himself now and then.”
“That's what I think,” said Sancho; “but now tell me, who was the first tumbler the world ever saw?”

“Honestly, brother,” the cousin answered, “I couldn't say for certain right at this moment without looking into it; I'll research the question when I get back to where my books are, and I'll satisfy you the next time we meet, since this won't be the last.”

“Look, señor,” said Sancho, “don't put yourself to any trouble over it, because I've just this minute hit on the answer to my own question. The first tumbler in the world, you should know, was Lucifer, when they threw or pitched him out of heaven; for he went tumbling all the way down into the bottomless pit.”
“You are right, friend,” said the cousin; and Don Quixote said, “Sancho, that question and that answer are not your own; you heard them from somebody else.”

“Hold your peace, señor,” said Sancho; “faith, if I start asking questions and answering them, I can keep going from now until tomorrow morning. No—when it comes to asking foolish things and answering with nonsense, I don't need to go borrowing help from the neighbors.”

“You have said more than you realize, Sancho,” said Don Quixote; “for there are people who wear themselves out learning and proving things which, once learned and proved, aren't worth a farthing to anyone's understanding or memory.”

In this and other pleasant talk the day slipped by, and that night they lodged in a little hamlet that lay, as the cousin told Don Quixote, no more than two leagues from the Cave of Montesinos; he added that if Don Quixote was determined to go inside, he would need to equip himself with ropes so that he could be tied and lowered into its depths. Don Quixote said that even if the cave went down to the bottomless pit itself, he meant to see where it ended; so they bought roughly a hundred fathoms of rope, and the next day at two in the afternoon they reached the cave, whose mouth is broad and spacious but so choked with thornbushes, wild fig, brambles, and briars, all thick and tangled together, that they close it off and cover it completely.

When the cave came into view, the cousin, Sancho, and Don Quixote dismounted, and the first two immediately bound the knight very securely with the ropes; and while they were strapping and wrapping him, Sancho said to him, “Watch what you're doing, master of mine; don't go burying yourself alive, or hanging yourself down there like a bottle lowered into a well to cool. It's no concern or business of your worship's to be the explorer of this place, which must be worse than a Moorish dungeon.”

“Tie me and hold your peace,” said Don Quixote, “for an enterprise like this, friend Sancho, was reserved for me;” and the guide said, “I beg you, Señor Don Quixote, to observe carefully and examine with a hundred eyes everything you find down there; perhaps there will be material I can put into my book of ‘Transformations.’”
“The drum is in hands that will know how to beat it,” said Sancho Panza.

When this was said and the tying finished (the ropes went not over his armor but over his doublet), Don Quixote remarked, “It was careless of us not to bring a small cattle-bell to fasten to the rope beside me; its sound would have told you I was still descending and still alive. But since that's out of the question now, may God's hand guide me;” and at once he dropped to his knees and offered up a quiet prayer to heaven, begging God to help him and grant him success in this apparently perilous and untried adventure. Then he cried aloud, “O mistress of my actions and my movements, illustrious and peerless Dulcinea del Toboso! If the prayers and pleas of this fortunate lover can possibly reach your ears, I implore you by your incomparable beauty to hear them; they ask nothing more than that you not deny me your favor and protection now, when I need them so badly. I am about to hurl myself, to sink, to plunge into the abyss that opens before me, solely to show the world that while you favor me there is no impossibility I will not attempt and achieve.” With these words he approached the chasm and saw that there was no way to lower himself or get in except by brute force or by hacking out a passage; so he drew his sword and began to slash and clear away the brambles at the mouth of the cave, and at the noise a huge multitude of crows and choughs burst out of it, so thick and so fast that they knocked Don Quixote flat; and if he had been as much a believer in omens as he was a Catholic Christian, he would have read it as a bad sign and refused to bury himself in such a place. But he got up, and since no more crows came out, nor any night-birds like the bats that had flown out along with the crows, the cousin and Sancho paid out the rope, and he lowered himself into the depths of the dreadful cavern. As he went in, Sancho sent his blessing after him, making a thousand signs of the cross over him and saying, “May God, and the Peña de Francia, and the Trinity of Gaeta guide you, flower and cream of knights-errant! There you go, daredevil of the earth, heart of steel, arm of brass; once more, God guide you and bring you back safe, sound, and unharmed to the light of this world you are leaving to bury yourself in the darkness you go looking for down there;” and the cousin offered up almost the same prayers and entreaties.

Don Quixote kept shouting up to them to give him rope and still more rope, and they fed it out little by little; and by the time his calls, which rose out of the cave as if through a pipe, could no longer be heard, they had paid out the entire hundred fathoms. They were of a mind to haul Don Quixote back up, since they had no more rope to give; still, they waited about half an hour, and at the end of that time they began drawing the rope in again with great ease, feeling no weight at all on it, which made them suspect that Don Quixote had stayed below; and convinced that this was so, Sancho wept bitterly and hauled away in a great hurry to find out the truth. But when they had pulled in what seemed to be a little more than eighty fathoms, they felt a weight, which delighted them enormously; and at last, after ten fathoms more, they saw Don Quixote plainly, and Sancho called out to him, “Welcome back, señor—we'd begun to think you were staying down there to start a family.” But Don Quixote answered not a word, and when they had drawn him all the way out they saw that his eyes were closed and that he looked, to all appearances, fast asleep.

They laid him on the ground and untied him, but still he did not wake; so they rolled him back and forth and shook him and tugged at him until, after a good while, he came to, stretching as though waking from a deep, heavy sleep. Looking around in apparent bewilderment, he said, “God forgive you, friends; you have torn me away from the sweetest and most delightful existence and spectacle any human being has ever known or beheld. Now indeed I understand that all the pleasures of this life pass like a shadow and a dream, or wither like the flower of the field. O ill-fated Montesinos! O sorely wounded Durandarte! O unhappy Belerma! O weeping Guadiana, and you, O luckless daughters of Ruidera, whose waters display the tears that once flowed from your beautiful eyes!”

The cousin and Sancho Panza listened with rapt attention to Don Quixote's words, which he uttered as though dragging them up from his very entrails with enormous pain. They begged him to explain himself and tell them what he had seen in that hell down below.
“Hell, you call it?” said Don Quixote; “don't give it any such name, for it doesn't deserve one, as you will soon see.”

He then asked them to give him something to eat, saying he was very hungry. They spread the cousin's sackcloth on the grass, raided the provisions in the alforjas, and all three, sitting down together in friendly and sociable fashion, made the meal serve as lunch and supper in one; and when the sackcloth had been cleared away, Don Quixote of La Mancha said, “Let no one rise; my sons, both of you, listen to me.”

title: Part 2, Chapter 23
paragraphs: About the wonderful things the incomparable Don Quixote said he saw in the deep cave of Montesinos — the impossibility and magnitude of which cause this adventure to be deemed apocryphal

It was about four in the afternoon when the sun, veiled in clouds, with softened light and tempered beams, let Don Quixote tell his two distinguished listeners what he had seen in the cave of Montesinos without heat or discomfort. He began as follows:

"About twelve or fourteen times a man's height down inside that pit, on the right-hand side, there's a recess or open space large enough to hold a big cart with its mules. A little light reaches it through some chinks or crevices that open to the surface of the earth. I noticed this recess when I was already growing tired and disgusted at finding myself hanging suspended by the rope, travelling downward into that dark region with no certainty or knowledge of where I was going. So I decided to enter it and rest for a while. I called out, telling you not to let out more rope until I gave the signal, but you must not have heard me. I then gathered in the rope you were sending me, made a coil of it, and sat down on it, thinking and considering what I should do to lower myself to the bottom, since I had no one to hold me up. And while I was deep in that perplexity, suddenly and without warning a profound sleep fell upon me, and when I least expected it — I don't know how — I woke and found myself in the middle of the most beautiful and delightful meadow that nature could produce or the most vivid human imagination conceive. I opened my eyes, I rubbed them, and I realised I was not asleep but thoroughly awake. Even so, I felt my head and chest to be sure it was really me there and not some empty deceiving phantom; but touch, feeling, and the steady thoughts running through my mind all convinced me that I was the same man then and there that I am at this moment. Next there appeared before my sight a stately royal palace or castle, with walls that seemed built of clear transparent crystal; and through two great doors which opened wide in it, I saw a venerable old man coming out and advancing toward me, dressed in a long mulberry-coloured serge gown that trailed on the ground. On his shoulders and chest he wore a green satin collegiate hood, and on his head a black Milanese bonnet; his snow-white beard fell below his belt. He carried no weapon at all, only a rosary of beads bigger than fair-sized hazelnuts, every tenth bead like a moderate ostrich egg; his bearing, his gait, his dignity and imposing presence held me spellbound and wondering. He came up to me, and the first thing he did was embrace me closely, and then he said, 'For a long time now, O valiant knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, we who are held enchanted in these solitudes have been hoping to see you, so that you might make known to the world what is shut up and hidden in this deep cavern, called the cave of Montesinos, which you have entered — an achievement reserved for your invincible heart and stupendous courage alone to attempt. Come with me, illustrious sir, and I will show you the marvels hidden within this transparent castle, of which I am the alcaide and perpetual warden; for I am Montesinos himself, from whom the cave takes its name.'

"The moment he told me he was Montesinos, I asked him if the story they tell up in the world above was true — that he had taken out the heart of his great friend Durandarte from his breast with a little dagger, and carried it to the lady Belerma, as his friend had commanded him at the point of death. He answered that they were right in every respect except about the dagger, since it was not a dagger, nor a little one, but a burnished poniard sharper than an awl."
"That poniard must have been made by Ramon de Hoces of Seville," said Sancho.

"I don't know," said Don Quixote; "but it could not have been made by that poniard-maker, because Ramon de Hoces was a man of yesterday, and the affair at Roncesvalles, where this mishap happened, was long ago. The question is of no great importance, though, and it doesn't affect or alter the truth or substance of the story."
"That's true," said the cousin; "go on, Señor Don Quixote, for I am listening to you with the greatest pleasure in the world."

"And I tell the tale with no less pleasure," said Don Quixote. "So, to continue — the venerable Montesinos led me into the crystal palace, where, in a lower chamber, strangely cool and made entirely of alabaster, there was an elaborately wrought marble tomb. Stretched at full length upon it I saw a knight — not of bronze, marble, or jasper, as are seen on other tombs, but of actual flesh and bone. His right hand (which struck me as somewhat hairy and sinewy, a sign of great strength in its owner) lay on the side of his heart. Before I could put any question to Montesinos, he, seeing me gazing at the tomb in amazement, said to me, 'This is my friend Durandarte, flower and mirror of the true lovers and valiant knights of his day. He is held enchanted here, as I myself and many others are, by that French enchanter Merlin who, they say, was the devil's son; but my belief is, not that he was the devil's son, but that he knew, as the saying is, a point more than the devil. How or why he enchanted us, no one knows; but time will tell, and I suspect that time is not far off. What I marvel at is this: I know it as surely as I know it's now day that Durandarte ended his life in my arms, and that after his death I took out his heart with my own hands — and it must have weighed more than two pounds, for, according to the naturalists, the man who has a large heart is more largely endowed with valour than the man who has a small one. Then how, given all that, and given that the knight really did die, does he now moan and sigh from time to time, as if he were still alive?'
"As he said this, the wretched Durandarte cried out in a loud voice:

O cousin Montesinos! 'Twas my last request of thee, When my soul hath left the body, And that lying dead I be, With thy poniard or thy dagger Cut the heart from out my breast, And bear it to Belerma. This was my last request."

"On hearing this, the venerable Montesinos fell on his knees before the unhappy knight and, with tearful eyes, exclaimed, 'Long since, Señor Durandarte, my beloved cousin, long since have I done what you bade me on that sad day when I lost you; I took out your heart as best I could, leaving not an atom of it in your breast. I wiped it with a lace handkerchief and took the road to France with it, having first laid you in the bosom of the earth with tears enough to wash and cleanse my hands of the blood that covered them after going through your innards. And, what's more, O cousin of my soul, at the first village I came to after leaving Roncesvalles, I sprinkled a little salt on your heart to keep it sweet, and bring it, if not fresh, at least pickled, into the presence of the lady Belerma — whom, together with you, myself, your squire Guadiana, the duenna Ruidera and her seven daughters and two nieces, and many more of your friends and acquaintances, the sage Merlin has kept enchanted here these many years. And although more than five hundred have gone by, not one of us has died; only Ruidera and her daughters and nieces are missing, and these, because of the tears they shed, Merlin — out of the compassion he seems to have felt for them — changed into so many lakes, which to this day in the world of the living, and in the province of La Mancha, are called the Lakes of Ruidera. The seven daughters belong to the kings of Spain and the two nieces to the knights of a very holy order called the Order of St. John. Your squire Guadiana, likewise bewailing your fate, was changed into a river of his own name; but when he came to the surface and saw the sun of another heaven, so great was his grief at finding he was leaving you that he plunged into the bowels of the earth. Since he cannot help following his natural course, however, he comes forth from time to time and shows himself to the sun and the world. The lakes I mentioned send him their waters, and with these, and others that come to him, he makes a grand and imposing entrance into Portugal; but for all that, wherever he goes he shows his melancholy and sadness, and takes no pride in breeding choice fish — only coarse and tasteless sorts, very different from those of the golden Tagus. All this that I'm telling you now, O cousin of mine, I have told you many times before; and since you make no answer, I fear that either you don't believe me or you don't hear me, which causes me God knows what grief. I have news to give you now which, if it doesn't serve to ease your suffering, will at least not increase it. Know that you have here before you (open your eyes and you will see) that great knight of whom the sage Merlin has prophesied such great things — that Don Quixote of La Mancha, I mean, who has again, and to better purpose than in past times, revived in these days the long-forgotten knight-errantry, and by whose intervention and aid we may yet be disenchanted; for great deeds are reserved for great men.'

"'And if that may not be,' said the wretched Durandarte in a low, feeble voice, 'if that may not be, then, my cousin, I say _patience and shuffle_;' and turning over on his side, he relapsed into his former silence without uttering another word."

"And now there was a great outcry and lamentation, accompanied by deep sighs and bitter sobs. I looked around, and through the crystal wall I saw a procession passing through another chamber — two lines of fair damsels all dressed in mourning, with white Turkish-style turbans on their heads. Behind them, in the rear, came a lady — for so her dignity made her seem — also dressed in black, with a white veil so long and full that it swept the ground. Her turban was twice as large as the largest of the others; her eyebrows met, her nose was rather flat, her mouth was large but with ruddy lips, and her teeth, of which she allowed an occasional glimpse, were seen to be sparse and badly set, though as white as peeled almonds. She carried in her hands a fine cloth, and in it, as well as I could make out, a heart that had been mummified, so parched and dried was it. Montesinos told me that all those in the procession were the attendants of Durandarte and Belerma, who were enchanted there with their master and mistress, and that the last one, the one carrying the heart in the cloth, was the lady Belerma. With her damsels, four days a week, she went in procession singing — or rather weeping — dirges over the body and miserable heart of his cousin; and if she appeared to me somewhat plain or not as beautiful as fame reported her, it was because of the bad nights and worse days she passed in that enchantment, as I could see from the great dark circles round her eyes and her sickly complexion. 'Her sallowness, and the rings round her eyes,' he said, 'are not caused by the monthly ailment usual with women — for it's been many months, even years, since she has had any — but by the grief her own heart suffers over the one she holds in her hand perpetually, which reminds her and brings back the sad fate of her lost lover. Were it not for this, hardly would the great Dulcinea del Toboso, so celebrated in all these parts and even in the world, come up to her in beauty, grace, and gaiety.'"

"'Hold hard!' I said at this. 'Tell your story as you ought, Señor Don Montesinos, for you know very well that all comparisons are odious, and there's no need to compare one person to another. The peerless Dulcinea del Toboso is what she is, and the lady Doña Belerma is what _she_ is and has been, and that's enough.' To which he replied, 'Forgive me, Señor Don Quixote; I own I was wrong, and spoke unadvisedly in saying that the lady Dulcinea could scarcely come up to the lady Belerma. It is enough for me to have learned, by what means I don't know, that you are her knight, to make me bite my tongue out before I would compare her to anything save heaven itself.' After this apology that the great Montesinos made me, my heart recovered from the shock it had taken at hearing my lady compared with Belerma."
"Still, I wonder," said Sancho, "that your worship didn't climb on the old fellow and bruise every bone of him with kicks, and pluck his beard until you didn't leave a hair in it."

"No, Sancho, my friend," said Don Quixote, "that would not have been right of me, for we are all bound to pay respect to the aged, even though they aren't knights — but especially to those who are, and who are enchanted. I only know I gave him as good as he brought in the many other questions and answers we exchanged."

"I can't understand, Señor Don Quixote," the cousin remarked here, "how it is that your worship, in such a short space of time as you have been below there, could have seen so many things, and said and answered so much."
"How long is it since I went down?" asked Don Quixote.
"Little more than an hour," replied Sancho.

"That can't be," returned Don Quixote, "because night overtook me while I was there, and day came, and it was night again and day again three times; so by my reckoning I have been three days in those remote regions beyond our ken."
"My master must be right," replied Sancho; "for since everything that has happened to him is by enchantment, maybe what seems to us an hour would seem three days and nights there."
"That's it," said Don Quixote.
"And did your worship eat anything all that time, señor?" asked the cousin.
"I never touched a morsel," answered Don Quixote, "nor did I feel hunger, or even think of it."
"And do the enchanted eat?" said the cousin.
"They neither eat," said Don Quixote, "nor are they subject to the grosser bodily needs, though it is thought their nails, beards, and hair do grow."
"And do the enchanted sleep, señor?" asked Sancho.
"Certainly not," replied Don Quixote; "at least, in the three days I was with them, not one of them closed an eye, nor did I either."

"The proverb 'Tell me what company you keep and I'll tell you what you are' fits the case here," said Sancho. "Your worship keeps company with enchanted people who are always fasting and watching; what wonder is it, then, that you neither eat nor sleep while you are with them? But forgive me, señor, if I say that of all this you've told us, may God take me — I was about to say the devil — if I believe a single particle."
"What!" said the cousin. "Has Señor Don Quixote been lying? Why, even if he wanted to, he hasn't had time to imagine and put together such a host of lies."
"I don't believe my master lies," said Sancho.
"If not, then what do you believe?" asked Don Quixote.

"I believe," replied Sancho, "that this Merlin, or those enchanters who enchanted the whole crowd your worship says you saw and spoke with down there, stuffed your imagination or your mind with all this rigmarole you've been treating us to, and all that's still to come."

"All that might be, Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "but it isn't so, because everything I've told you I saw with my own eyes and touched with my own hands. But what will you say when I tell you now how, among the countless other marvellous things Montesinos showed me (of which at the proper time, in the course of our journey, I will give you an account, for they wouldn't all fit here), he showed me three country girls who went skipping and capering like goats across the pleasant fields there — and the instant I saw them I knew one to be the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso, and the other two those same country girls who were with her, the ones we spoke to on the road from El Toboso? I asked Montesinos if he knew them, and he said he did not, but he thought they must be some enchanted ladies of distinction, for they had only made their appearance in those meadows a few days before. I was not to be surprised at that, because there were a great many other ladies there, of times past and present, enchanted in various strange shapes — and among them he had recognised Queen Guinevere and her dame Quintañona, the one who poured out the wine for Lancelot when he came from Britain."

When Sancho Panza heard his master say this, he was ready to take leave of his senses, or die laughing. Since he knew the real truth about the pretended enchantment of Dulcinea — having himself been the enchanter and the concocter of all the evidence — he made up his mind at last that, beyond all doubt, his master was out of his wits and stark mad. So he said to him, "It was an evil hour, a worse season, and a sorrowful day, dear master mine, when your worship went down to the other world, and an unlucky moment when you met Señor Montesinos, who has sent you back to us like this. You were well enough up here in your full senses, such as God had given you, delivering maxims and giving advice at every turn — not as you are now, talking the greatest nonsense imaginable."
"As I know you, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "I pay no attention to your words."

"Nor I to your worship's," said Sancho, "whether you beat me or kill me for the ones I've spoken, or will speak, if you don't correct and mend your own. But tell me, while we're still at peace, how or by what did you recognise the lady our mistress? And if you spoke to her, what did you say, and what did she answer?"

"I recognised her," said Don Quixote, "by her wearing the same garments she had on when you pointed her out to me. I spoke to her, but she didn't utter a word in reply; on the contrary, she turned her back on me and took to flight at such a pace that a crossbow bolt couldn't have overtaken her. I wanted to follow her, and would have, had Montesinos not advised me not to bother, as it would be useless, particularly since the time was drawing near when I'd have to leave the cavern. He told me, moreover, that in time he would let me know how he and Belerma, and Durandarte, and all who were there, were to be disenchanted. But of all I saw and observed down there, what gave me most pain was this: while Montesinos was speaking to me, one of the two companions of the hapless Dulcinea came up to me on one side without my having seen her coming, and with tears in her eyes said to me, in a low, agitated voice, 'My lady Dulcinea del Toboso kisses your worship's hands and begs you to do her the favour of letting her know how you are; and, being in great need, she also begs your worship as earnestly as she can to be so good as to lend her half a dozen reals — or as much as you may have on you — on this new dimity petticoat I have here; and she promises to repay them very soon.' I was amazed and taken aback by such a message, and turning to Señor Montesinos I asked him, 'Is it possible, Señor Montesinos, that persons of distinction under enchantment can be in need?' To which he replied, 'Believe me, Señor Don Quixote, what is called need is to be met with everywhere, and penetrates all quarters and reaches everyone, and does not spare even the enchanted; and since the lady Dulcinea del Toboso sends to ask for those six reals, and the pledge is to all appearance a good one, there's nothing for it but to give them to her, for no doubt she must be in some great strait.' 'I will take no pledge from her,' I replied, 'nor can I give her what she asks, for all I have is four reals' — which I gave (they were the ones you, Sancho, gave me the other day to hand out as alms to the poor I met along the road) — 'and I said, Tell your mistress, my dear, that I am grieved to the heart over her distresses, and wish I were a Fugger to remedy them, and that I would have her know that I cannot, and ought not to, be in good health while deprived of the happiness of seeing her and enjoying her discreet conversation; and that I implore her as earnestly as I can to allow herself to be seen and addressed by this captive servant and forlorn knight of hers. Tell her too that when she least expects it she will hear it announced that I have made an oath and vow after the fashion of the one the Marquis of Mantua made to avenge his nephew Baldwin when he found him at the point of death in the heart of the mountains — namely, not to eat bread off a tablecloth, and other trifling matters which he added, until he had avenged him; and I will make the same vow, to take no rest and to roam the seven regions of the earth more thoroughly than the Infante Don Pedro of Portugal ever roamed them, until I have disenchanted her.' 'All that and more you owe my lady,' was the damsel's answer to me; and taking the four reals, instead of curtseying she cut a caper, springing two full yards into the air."

"O blessed God!" exclaimed Sancho aloud at this. "Is it possible that such things can be in the world, and that enchanters and enchantments can have such power in it as to have changed my master's right senses into a craze so full of absurdity? O señor, señor, for God's sake, think of yourself, have a care for your honour, and give no credit to this silly stuff that has left you scant and short of wits."

"You talk this way because you love me, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "and not being experienced in the things of the world, everything that has some difficulty about it seems to you impossible. But time will pass, as I said before, and I will tell you some of the things I saw down there that will make you believe what I've related now, the truth of which admits of neither reply nor question."

title: Part 2, Chapter 24
paragraphs: Wherein are related a thousand trifling matters, as trivial as they are necessary to the right understanding of this great history

The man who translated this great history from the original written by its first author, Cide Hamete Benengeli, says that on coming to the chapter giving the adventures of the cave of Montesinos he found these exact words written in the margin in Hamete's own hand:

"I cannot convince or persuade myself that everything written in the preceding chapter could have happened precisely to the valiant Don Quixote — and for this reason: that all the adventures that have occurred up to now have been possible and probable; but as for this one of the cave, I see no way of accepting it as true, since it passes all reasonable bounds. To believe that Don Quixote could lie, he being the most truthful gentleman and the noblest knight of his time, is impossible; he would not have told a lie though he were shot to death with arrows. On the other hand, I reflect that he related and told the story with all the details given, and that he could not in so short a space have fabricated such a vast complication of absurdities. If, then, this adventure seems apocryphal, that's no fault of mine; and so, without affirming its falsehood or its truth, I write it down. Decide for yourself in your wisdom, reader; I am not bound, nor is it in my power, to do more — though it's certain they say that at the time of his death he retracted, and said he had invented it, thinking it matched and fitted the adventures he had read of in his histories." And then he goes on to say:

The cousin was amazed both at Sancho's boldness and at the patience of his master, and concluded that the good temper Don Quixote displayed came from the happiness he felt at having seen his lady Dulcinea, even enchanted as she was; because otherwise the words and language Sancho had used to him deserved a thrashing, for he really did seem to have been rather impudent. Now the cousin said to him, "I, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, look upon the time I have spent in travelling with your worship as very well spent, for I have gained four things from it. The first is that I have made your acquaintance, which I consider great good fortune; the second, that I have learned what the cave of Montesinos contains, together with the transformations of the Guadiana and of the lakes of Ruidera — which will be useful to me for the Spanish Ovid I have in hand; the third, to have discovered the antiquity of cards — that they were in use at least in the time of Charlemagne, as may be inferred from the words you say Durandarte uttered when, at the end of that long spell while Montesinos was talking to him, he woke up and said, 'Patience and shuffle.' He could not have learned that phrase and expression while he was enchanted, only before he became so, in France, in the time of the said emperor Charlemagne. And this demonstration is just the thing for that other book I'm writing, the 'Supplement to Polydore Vergil on the Invention of Antiquities;' for I believe he never thought of including cards in his book, as I mean to do in mine — and it will be a matter of great importance, particularly when I can cite so grave and truthful an authority as Señor Durandarte. And the fourth thing is that I have established the source of the river Guadiana, until now unknown to mankind."
"You are right," said Don Quixote; "but I'd like to know, if by God's favour they grant you a licence to print those books of yours — which I doubt — to whom do you mean to dedicate them?"
"There are lords and grandees in Spain to whom they can be dedicated," said the cousin.

"Not many," said Don Quixote; "not that they are unworthy of it, but because they don't care to accept books and take on the obligation of making the return that seems due to the author's labour and courtesy. One prince I know who makes up for all the rest, and more — how much more, if I ventured to say, would perhaps stir up envy in many a noble breast; but let this stand over for some more convenient time, and let's go and look for some place to shelter ourselves in tonight."

"Not far from here," said the cousin, "there is a hermitage where a hermit lives who they say was once a soldier, and who has the reputation of being a good Christian and a very intelligent and charitable man. Next to the hermitage he has a small house that he built at his own cost, but though small it's large enough to receive guests."
"Has this hermit any hens, do you think?" asked Sancho.

"Few hermits are without them," said Don Quixote; "for those we see nowadays are not like the hermits of the Egyptian deserts, who dressed in palm-leaves and lived on the roots of the earth. But don't think that by praising these I am disparaging the others; all I mean is that the penances of those today don't come up to the asceticism and austerity of former times; but it doesn't follow from this that they are not all worthy — at least I think them so; and at the worst, the hypocrite who pretends to be good does less harm than the open sinner."

At this point they saw a man on foot approaching the spot where they stood, moving at a rapid pace and beating a mule loaded with lances and halberds. When he came up to them he greeted them and passed on without stopping. Don Quixote called to him, "Stay, good fellow; you seem to be in more of a hurry than suits that mule."

"I cannot stop, señor," the man answered; "the arms you see I'm carrying here are to be used tomorrow, so I mustn't delay. God be with you. But if you want to know what I am carrying them for, I mean to lodge tonight at the inn beyond the hermitage, and if you're going the same way you will find me there, and I will tell you some curious things. Once more, God be with you;" and he urged his mule on at such a pace that Don Quixote had no time to ask what these curious things were that he meant to tell them. Since Don Quixote was somewhat inquisitive and always tortured by his anxiety to learn something new, he decided to set out at once and pass the night at the inn instead of stopping at the hermitage, where the cousin had wanted them to halt. So they mounted, and all three took the direct road for the inn, which they reached a little before nightfall. On the way the cousin proposed that they go up to the hermitage for a quick drink. The moment Sancho heard this he steered his Dapple toward it, and Don Quixote and the cousin did the same. But it seems Sancho's bad luck so ordered it that the hermit was not at home, for so a sub-hermit they found at the hermitage told them. They called for some of the best. She replied that her master had none, but that if they liked cheap water she would give it with great pleasure.
"If I'd been after water," said Sancho, "there are wells along the road where I could have had enough of it. Ah, Camacho's wedding, and the plentiful house of Don Diego — how I miss you!"

Leaving the hermitage, they pushed on toward the inn, and a little further on they came upon a youth who was walking ahead of them at no great speed, so they overtook him. He carried a sword over his shoulder, with a bundle slung on it — apparently his clothes, probably his breeches or trousers, and his cloak and a shirt or two; for he had on a short jacket of velvet with a satiny gloss in places, and his shirt was hanging out; his stockings were silk, and his shoes square-toed in the court style. He might have been eighteen or nineteen, with a merry face and an apparently energetic manner, and he walked along singing seguidillas to lighten the tedium of the road. As they came up with him he was just finishing one, which the cousin learned by heart and which is said to run as follows —
I'm off to the wars For the want of pence, Oh, had I but money I'd show more sense.
The first to address him was Don Quixote, who said, "You travel very lightly, sir gallant; where are you bound, may we ask, if it's your pleasure to tell us?"
To which the youth replied, "The heat and my poverty are the reason for my travelling so lightly, and it's to the wars that I'm bound."
"How poverty?" asked Don Quixote; "the heat one can understand."

"Señor," replied the youth, "in this bundle I'm carrying velvet trousers to match this jacket; if I wear them out on the road, I won't be able to make a decent appearance in them in the city, and I haven't the money to buy others; so for this reason, as well as to keep myself cool, I'm making my way in this fashion to catch up with some companies of infantry that are not twelve leagues off, in which I'll enlist; and after that there will be no lack of baggage trains to travel with to the place of embarkation, which they say will be Cartagena. I'd rather have the King for a master, and serve him in the wars, than serve some court pauper."
"And did you get any bonus, now?" asked the cousin.

"If I had been in the service of some grandee of Spain or some distinguished personage," replied the youth, "I'd surely have got it; for that's the advantage of serving good masters — out of the servants' hall men come to be ancients or captains, or get a good pension. But to my misfortune I always served place-hunters and adventurers whose keep and wages were so miserable and scanty that half went on paying for the starching of one's collars; it would be a miracle indeed if a page-volunteer ever got anything like a reasonable bonus."
"And tell me, for heaven's sake," asked Don Quixote, "is it possible, my friend, that in all the time you served you never got any livery?"

"They gave me two," replied the page; "but just as when you leave a religious community before taking your vows, they strip you of the dress of the order and give you back your own clothes — so did my masters return mine to me. As soon as the business that had brought them to court was finished, they went home and took back the liveries they had given merely for show."

"What _spilorceria_, as an Italian would say," said Don Quixote; "but for all that, consider yourself happy in having left court with as worthy an object as you have, for there's nothing on earth more honourable or more profitable than serving, first of all God, and then one's king and natural lord, particularly in the profession of arms — by which, if not more wealth, at least more honour is to be won than by letters, as I have said many a time. For though letters may have founded more great houses than arms, still those founded by arms have I know not what superiority over those founded by letters, and a certain splendour belonging to them that distinguishes them above all. And bear in mind what I'm about to say to you, for it will be of great use and comfort to you in time of trouble: don't let your mind dwell on the bad chances that may befall you, for the worst of all is death, and if it is a good death, the best of all is to die. They asked Julius Caesar, the valiant Roman emperor, what was the best death. He answered, the unexpected one, the one that comes suddenly and unforeseen; and though he answered like a pagan and one without knowledge of the true God, still, as far as sparing our feelings is concerned, he was right; for suppose you're killed in the first engagement or skirmish, whether by a cannonball or blown up by a mine — what does it matter? It's only dying, and all is over. According to Terence, a soldier looks better dead in battle than alive and safe in flight; and the good soldier wins fame in proportion as he is obedient to his captains and those in command over him. And remember, my son, that it's better for the soldier to smell of gunpowder than of civet, and that if old age should come upon you in this honourable calling — though you may be covered with wounds and crippled and lame — it will not come upon you without honour, and such as poverty cannot lessen; especially now that provisions are being made for supporting and relieving old and disabled soldiers. For it isn't right to deal with them after the fashion of those who set free and get rid of their black slaves when they are old and useless, turning them out of their houses under the pretence of making them free and making them slaves to hunger, from which they cannot expect to be released except by death.
